div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
WY DRAB. Nzuaz,

Some charming effects in millinery are now to be seen. Everything tends towards lightness, as op- posed to the somewhat heavy hats we have seen in all black for the past month. Toques of white tulle tulle or crin, are veiled in black lacq.or lighted-jetted tulle, with black and white aigrettes atone side, and black leaves and ferns will be much used in conjunction with white hats and toques. One, which is perfect in its elegant simplicity, is worthy of notice. It consists of a large toquet of White cr' in in layers raised up one above another, and veiled with white tulle over the whole, sweep- ingoright round from back to front being a large way of black maidenhair, powdered with jet. Experience has taught that nothing really surpasses the magpie mixture for chic effects.

There is little fear of the blouse going out of fashion. The blouse, though its demise is pre- dicted with confidence every year, seems destined to prolong its days to a good old age. The slip will be even more popular than last year, in rich white satin, with yokepiece, neckband, and cuffs of guipure. For country and town alike, with a white or a black skirt, nothing distances the simple elegance of this slip blouse; in cream it looks its best though it is to be had in black, mauve, and colours. There is a new make of sleeve for taffetas shirts which is very striking, and much smarter than the pagoda; it is cut like a bishop's sleeve, rather smaller at the shoulder and top part of the arm than below the elbow, then set into a narrow band at the wrist, above which it is slashed to show an under-sleeve of puffed muslin, overlaced with gold cords.

White and cream-coloured lace will enjoy an even greater vogue than they did last year. The absence of colour in dress will bring them more prominently into favour. There is no doubt that, -after the stated period for wearing mourning shall haVe expired, there will be a fashion of black and white throughout the season. This would scarcely be a novelty. Some five years since there was =oh a rage for black and white that it became almost a livery of the well-dressed. Striped materials in the two negative colours are being 7i.anufactured in quantities to be ready for ths \ge demand expected.

Chatelaine bags will continue in favour so long as the vogue of tight-fitting skirts lasts. A smart bag can be made of black satin ornamented with an appliquifeof pale grey kid outlined with little silver-sequins. The bag is made in two pieces mounteation stiff card, each piece being shaped as an oval with one—the top—end cut straight across. When the ornamented satin has been strained over the GaAs they are joined with a puffing of black soft silk(with which the bag is also lined) and a frill and draw-strings of black satin ribbon with silver tags added at the top. With regard to embroidering lace with jewels there is no denying that when it is 110 to overdone the effect is good, partly because of the mysterious way in which the glitter seems to come from no- where. Same of the lace is sewn with pearls, and on one ball dress the white satin foundation is covered with imitation point richly sawn with pearls and lined with gold gauze. While any amount of ingenuity and originality may be expended upon the sleeves of new frocks, the simpler patterns are going to prevail. Of °nor- . mous pagoda puffs there have been many, and oi pouched elbows, but what could be prettier than a slit in the inner side of the sleeve, inlet with soft lace, mousseline, or silk caught together here and there?

Steel is to be very fashionable again this season, and will be found extremely useful as a half- mourning trimming. Its beauty would be better appreciated if it were not so inexpensive a material. At some of the recent fashionable weddings it has been seen on toques, and a novel ruffle is black silk, the edges sewn with loops of cut steel beads. Sallow people, to whom black is unbecoming, will find that a cut-steel necklet removes all its dis- advantages in this way. There is something in the sparkle of the silvery grey that brings out any latent pink in the cheeks and increases the bright- ness of the i eyes. Steel ornaments look uncom- monly well n grey or white hair. Home embroiderers work well in steel, producing effects equal to anything that comes from abroad. If only Englishwomen with money and a taste for pretty things- would give English workers a chance ! But it almeet.seems tia.:.6 this is the very last thing that they incline to do.
Your loving JrNms.
There le Security in
A fon •mons tho. toothbrast
every morning

div.head: Mc DOUG
div.p: Mc DOUG
WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Royal Buckhounds are to go at last and in their place the King will maintain a pack of Ro3 at Foxhounsa Instead of setting up new kennels, it is thought that the King will take over the Garth hounds,which are located at Haines Hall, Twyford, and hunt that part of Berk shire nearest to Windsor Castle, and which is easily accessible from London. The King and Queen however will not be much at Windsor until next year. The re- decoration and alterations at the Castle will take quite twelve months, and while this work is in progress, the ring and Queen will reside at Frogmsre Lodse during their visits to Windsor. Among other changes, there is to be a great removal of the old-fashioned and inartistic) furniture at the Castle, and at other Royal Residences which will be replaced by that of new designs more in accord with mooern taste. It can easily be understeod that the exclusiveness which attaches to the Theone, is not a little irksome to the Ring. As Prince of Wales, be had a charming, free and easy manner in scciety, but in one stress+ this free- eom is no longer possible, arid even among his most intimate acquaintances there is a reserve imposed which must be in strange contrast with the friendly cordiality I of former days. Of course this change in social relatisn- ships squally applies to the Queen, who, it is no secret was happier at Sindriegham and Marlborough House, than at Windsor Castle and Buckingham Palace. The King's time is now much more taken up with State affairs, which no doubt afford him some relief for the less of amusements, and intimate acquaintances which the recuit change must mean to His Mijesty. It is advised thst new applications should be made by societies and institutions which enjoyed the patrenage or Queen Victoria, or ot the King, or Queen Alexandra, when they were Prince and Princess of Wales It is unnecessary to remark that royal patronage is of very powerful assistance to any institution, and that, by increasing the public confidence in the management, it is the means of bringing in much larger subscriptions than would otherwise be obtained. In the vast majority of cases, that patronage is bestowed wisely, but whilst one is anxious not to say anything ill-natured, at thei same time it would be well in some cases to institute 1 inquiries before the patronage is renewed, particularly among these societies which have no treasurer, and invite the despatch of subscriptions, to the one person who undertakes the expenditure. The first public event patronised by the King and Qceen since their accessioa, was the sale and exhibition of the Irish Industries Association, which was held on the 19th and 20th inst. at Grosvenor House, the town residence of the Duke and Duchess of Westminster. Last year the sale was held at the Mansion House,in and on tomer occasions they have teken place at the Londonderry House, Devonshire House, and also at Brighton, Liverpool, and other planes. Altogether these pales have produced nearly £25,000 besidi s about £30,000 which bas been taken at the depot of the Associstion in Motcombe-street. Lady Londonderry, Lady Lansdowne, Lady Devonshire, Lady Mayo, the Duchess of Abercorn, and others well-known in Dublin and London Society, have been chiefly instrumental in making the Irish Industries Asscciation a success. The Marchioness of Dufferin will probably perform the ceremony of christening the Shamro k 11, Sir Thomas Lipton's new challenger for the American Cup. The launch is expected to take place next month, as the,two Shamrocks are to appear together, arid its open contests on the Clyde, in the races to be held early la June in connection with the Glasgow exhibition. The usual se- crecy has been observed in the construction of the mew Shamrock. but Sir Thomas Lipton, who says his first at tempt taught him many valuable lessons, is confident of his chances this year. Hitherto the many attempts to capture the American Cup have been very much like capturing De Wet, but there will consequently be all the ' more rejoicing should Sir Thomas Lipton succeed at last I in wresting the prize from the Americans. Many women in search of husbands or excitement, have turned their thoughts to South Africa, which is popularly supposed to be the premised land of million- aires. These however do not belong to the class which Mr Chamberlain had in his mind when speaking the ether day on behalf of the United British Women's As sociation. Mr Chamberlain believes there will shortly be a great mall of men to South Africa, and he strongly advocated that country as a field for women, who were prepared to emigrate,and settle in the Colonies. Whether farm life on the veldt is one that has much attraction for women, may perhaps be open to question. It is those who are prepared to fate the hardships and ieolation of country life, velum Mr Chamberlain would like to see mettle in the new colonies, the same as British and Irish women have Settled in Natal, but there is also no doubt that there are many openicgs for working women of all classes in South Atrica. in any case the Women's Emigration Association has done excellent work as a benevolent institution. It is worthy of sup- port trom those who are disposed to pecuniarily assist in its good work, and it may be trusted by all who seek its help and advice. The gift of a Royal Standard and ensign frcm the London firemen must have been particularly acceptable to the Duke of Cornwall and York, seeing that most of the firemen are old naval men, and are commanded by a sailor. They are an extremely smart body of men, and Many striking gosh a are related of the alertness which they display in getting away to fires, and of their resource in poeitiots of exceptional difficulty. His Royal Highness assured Commander Wells that the flags will be used on occasions of ceremony, during the cruise of the Ophir, and they will no doubt be an object of interest to the firemen of the colonies. Concerning the outfit of the Duchess of Cornwall and York, three items at least will help to guide those about to order new frocks. To begin with, the bolero appears on nearly all Her Royal Highness's gowns in one form or another, then mope de chine (i.f English weavine) is utilised extensively both for day and evening toilettrs, while for the latter,theivery short sleeves only have been decided on. Much has been said of late about the dis- appearance at fashionable functions of the abort sleeve, bet the fact that the Queen, and the Duchess of Corn- wall still cling to it, will an more than enough to insure the mode a fresh lease of popularity. In Dame, the tiouse has disappeared, but In name only, for this very useful article is still in the highest favour under the title of " corsage." The very latest have no bones at all,and are lined with Barnett lug pliable and warm. The new soft }bidets biiks are being widely employed for spring " Corsages," and these fabrics can- not be too highly praised both from an artistic and economic point of view. It is now possible to secure them in the most delicate aid beautiful self-cnlours, a vast improvement on the striped varieties at one time the only kind availeble. Glace silk shirts are particularly smelt wear just mow, and these, it is almost unnecessary to add, are invariably tucked, gauged, or stitched, sometimes all three. Many women who thornugly understand the art of dress, are dispensing with the popular yoge in front, preferring the lines carried up to the shoulders. This is usquestionablo the more beeornieg idea to the majority, who can ill-afford to dispense with the extra length the absence of the yoke in front gives. As to lace—the craze for this is as prevalent as ever. Any kind is modish, but at the moment preference is being shown for the Irish needle point. Limerick, and the Crochets usually called point d' Ireland. There is also a fashion in veils, and the diecerning among us bestow as much att,- ration on this accessory, as we do on our hats and teepee. Ttie ebenillo spot still comes first, and some of the newest French varieties, which are of the finest mesh, thereby making the spots appear unsupported, are finished off with lace-trimmed ledges, which, keened at the back of the hatSfall grace- fully on the hair behind. The lace veils which have appearel from time to time during the winter season, are little donned, the cfliict upon thelairest of wearers being undesirable to a degree.
" MADGE."

WARRINGION PERMANENT' BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY.
A Reduced Dividend.

The annual meeting of the above named society was held in Cairn-street School on Thursday last week. Mr James Benwortoy (the president), occupied the chair, and there were also present : Messrs John Critchley. Thomas Critchley, John Dewhurst, Thomas Ince,George Legge, John Mather, P C Price, and R Shackleton (directors), Aquila Cook (treasurer), William Dick (auditor), Thomas Prowl (secretary), W J Shaw, W Dalin w, Cook, Joseph Podmore, Joseph Podmore jun., Perrin!, A Longshaw, and others, THE CHAIRMAN AND "SINISTER REPORTS."

The directors presented their 34th annual statement of accounts and declared a dividend of al per cent. The CaammaN in moving the adoption of the report went fully into the Society's financial position. He pointed out that the Society had been in existence for 34 years, it having been established in 1867. The capital very soon reached £90,000 and since that time the diree- tore bad been nayihg off at the rate of some- thing like £2,000 each year and that had gone on up to the present time. Mr John Critchley and he (the chairman) were the two oldest directors and when they joined the directorate the capi- tal of the society was £70,000. Since then it had been reduced to just below £40,000. In recent years, build- ing societies had not load the same run as when the society was first established and they now considered a £40,000 society a very good society. (Hear, hear.) Their society was in a very good condition. He made those remarks that evening because of reports which had been circulated during the past year. He did not say they had been wilfully circulated, but certain per- sons had circulated reports to the detriment of the society which would not bear examination. --He wished to call attention to the property in hand. The original valuation of the property was £41,812 and the amount owing to the society was £34.167, leaving a balance in favour of the society of £7.645. If they added to that the sum of £1,600. the amoun:. of the reserve fund,they had a total of £9,371 in favour of the society. They might therefore say that the money advanced was 75 per cent of the total value. He did not know of a building society which te as in the happy position of only having advanced three-quarters of the value of the property to those who bad borrowed the money. When the property fell into the society 's hands it was generally because the people who owned it either could not or would not pay up the subscriptions due, and therefore they were always to a certain extent in arrears before they took possession. Then there was I that bug-bear of street-making which had perhap. I brought more property into the society's hands than I anything else,because when they applied to the directors for a further advance for street making the directors were unable to make it without more security, and con- sequently the owners gave up the security rather than attempt to pay anything. These streets had been paid for by the society and in addition to that the members must remembor th it fire insurance societies were send lug out circulars that owing to the extraordinary cast oe buildings at the present time the payments for insurano ought to be increased at least by 15 or 20 per cent. Turning to another item in the balance sheet, the chairman pointed out that the amount of advances by the society was £36,890, whilst the amount owing on the same was £34, 167, , being a decrease of over £2,000 since the Society took ' possession of them. Referring to the year's work he said it was a little disappointing, because th sinister reports bad had two effects on the Society. They had made a large number give notice for the w.thdrawal ox their shares, and they had also prevented others from investing, so that they had cut against the Society in two ways. The consequeece was that the directors bad had to refuse good business—business they could never have doubted for a moment—but they had not the money to do it with. The interest, Sm., during the past year bad only totalled up to £1,320 21 11d, whilst last year it was over £1,500. 90 far as the directors could see there was no possibility or p-obability of that interest decreasing, but on the contrary the,, believed it would gradually go back again to theiold figure. After paying the management expenses there was £1,016 9s 41 from which the ditec'ors could declare a dividend. Under the circumstances of the case it was a very difficult matter for the directors to arrive at a dccision that would be satis- factvry. Some directors were of opinion—and he must admit he was one of them—that it would be almost best not to pay any dividend at all but carry the £1,016 to the reserve fund. That had been done by almost every society in existence at one time or another, but their society bad never adopted that plan and the director came to the conclusion not to adopt it now, mainly on the ground that many of tte investors were persons cl« pending to a great extent on the usual interest of their money. It was accordingly decided to pay a reduced dividend of 2i per ceat.which was the present bank int,rest. That would leave them a balance in band of £250 to be carried forward to the reserve fund. It would have been possible to pay another one per cent dividend but still it was thought better to increase the reserve fund even if they had to pay a less dividend this year. (Hear, hear.) He thought the society would tide over its present difficulties. It was not the first time an unfavourable rumour bad affected the society and it had been tided over, and the directors hoped that the present one would be tided over in the hitt rests of , the shareholders. (Applause.) I Mr DALLow seconded the adoption of the report. . .

_ Mr Klexcowarat, proceeded to explain in detail the fioarcial position of toe society and bore out the Chair- man's statement as to its sound-ess. He believed that the street malting to which alusicn had been made was nes ly completed go far as the society's property was c ncerned and therefore the society ceuld expect more income from all sources. The rtpr rts which had been circulated were absolorply wrong and unfounded. The society was well ,ffic,ro-cl snri the directors deserved sympathy, supp.rt and Co•op, ration instead of censure. (Hear, hear.) He would advise Chi in not to swop horses when crossing a stream. I Mr W J .i.2ltaxv referred to th. rumours which bad

been circulated and stated that they made him Teel ur - easy. When he g+ve) rotice for his capital, to Ws "gr,. t horror and surprise " he found he could not get it,as be would have to wait his turn for the money to be paid in. Be thought it was a great hardship, especially to the small investors who were obliged to wait over twelve months before they could receive their money. The society ought to consider whe, her it was justified in con- tinuing to receive small investments from poor people when it was probable that they would have to wait pro- bably two or three years. There were notices which wore handed in over a year ago and the money bad not yet been paid. In conclusion, be would like to ask the secretary what further sums were likely to be spent en street making ? The SECRETARY : There is only one street that is not mado and that is Ear'-street. It will cost between £5O and £6O The CHAIRMAN, in replying to the observations of Mr Shaw, said when people invested tkeir money in a building society they did not want it putting in the I bank in order that they might get it back as soon as they wanted it. The directors were obliged to invest it in mortgage securities. 'lb society tilsi something like £55,000 invested in property, and they were not going I to sell the property at a loss in order to pay off those who had given notice. The report was sdop"ed. ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The neat busirTess-W-ae the e (1 three directors, The retiring directors were Ne-ers John Critehler- Thenvis Critchley and P C Price, and they offered them. selves tor re-election. The three gentlemen named were imanimoualy re-elected. Mr Aquil a Cock was re-alected treasurer ; Mr William Twigs, surveyor ; and Mr James Bolton, F.8.A.A., and Mr William Dick, auditors.
TOTE OF THANKS.

Mr KIIIKCONNEL prepileti a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and referred in felicitous terms to Mr Ben worthy's services. The CHAIRMAN, in ackno ledging the compliment. said he bad aiwiys endravcured to do what be believed tl be the righv. fot the interests of the society in general.

RUBY LOVEDAY.
By SILAS K. HOCKING, Author of "The Strange Adventures. of. Israel Pendray," "The Day of Recompense," "God's . Outcast," "In Spite of Fate," "He; Benny," • _
CIIAPTER XXIII. THE ATTACK. ' "How the Right of means to do ill deeds, Make ill deeds done,"

Mr. Bice was not long in discovering that the whole of the Pentyre family occupied positions at the upstairs windows. This was reassuring. It implied that the resistance was to be passive rather than active. There was no sign of guns or of any other deadly weapon. Violence on the part of the Pentyres did not appear to be on their programme. Mr. Bice drew a long breath and began to breathe freely. He was not devoid of courage, but he objected, nevertheless, to being shot at from behind a barricade.

Within a few paces of the front door he paused and looked up at John, who sat at the open window directly above his head. "Then you • are determiusd to resist the law?" he questioned. "Igo, I am not," was the quick reply, "but I'm determined to resist you." "But I have brought, as you see, the officers of the law with me."

"I can't help that." "But you are foolish to hold out. You have been served with legal notice to quit. You haven't a leg to stand on, either in law or equity. If you won't go out quietly, we are bound-to put you out by force. lam sorry to have to do it. But the house is let to another tenant who is waiting to come in."

"You've no right to let what isn't yours," John said, doggedly. "And as for putting us out by force, well, that's a game that two can play at." "But you know what resisting the law officers means? You won't find Bodmin Gaol a particularly comfortable place to live in." "I'm prepared to take my chance of it in any case."

"Then you won't open the door?" "No, I won't," and John stamped on the floor which was a signal to those below. Tom Penda,x7is, with the nozzle of his hose in position was getting impatient for the talk to end. He was afraid that the tubing would burst, so. strong was the weight of water behind. Mr. Bice's mouth fell open at John's last reply, and he appeared for a moment to be in a brown study. Tom heard the signal overhead and turned the tap. The torrent ,of water leaped out swift and, straight as a shaft of light. Torn'ii aim was accurate. Mr. Bice's open mouth was full to overflowing in a moment. With a gasp and a splutter he sprang a full foot from the ' ground, the swift jet of water following him and smacking him in the eyes, on the cheeks, and rattling on the starch of his immaculate shirt front. .As soon as he could recover his breath he yelled at the top of his voice, a yell which was caught up by the crowd and ended in a roar of derisive laughter. The policemen endeavoured to take action at once, but a stinging torrent of water straight in their faces was not at all conducive to clearness of vision. They tried bravely to shield their faces with their hands, but no chain gun ever delivered its charges with such rapidity or with such effect as this quick-firing hose. They' ran first this way, then that, gasping, !puttering, swearing, the relentless torrent follow- ing them, deafening them, blinding them, and reducing their courage to the consistency of their clothes. The Pentyrell at the upstairs windows laughed till the tears ran down their faces. Such a panto- mime they had never seen before, their only regret being that it was so soon over. The crowd, which by this time had grown ,to considerable dimensions, laughed, and yelled, and clapped their hands, and almost went into hysterics, while the inglorious three beat a hasty retreat towards the garden gate. "Now officers pluck up your courage and do your duty," cried a wag in the crowd. "Shoulder arms and march." But the policemen were too crestfallen even to retort. "Let the women bind up their'wounds," some- one else shouted; "the poor fellows are ready to faint and die," and the crowd yelled again. "Look at old Bice's shirt front," yelled a small boy. "Won't his mother beat him ! So to a running fire of ridicule and derisive laughter they made their way down the lane as fast as their soaked and clinging clothes would let them. At the bottom their horse and trap were waiting for them, and, climbing into the vehicle with most unseemly haste, they were driven swiftly. away in the direction of Trelford. John Pentyre and his family came out into the garden and held a levee. But Tom Pendarvis kept resolutely out of sight, and no one in St. lago, Churchtown, knew yet that he had returned. • John was greatly touched by the sympathy of his. neighbours, and offers of assistance flowed in upon him from every side." "I shall not need your help to-day, at any rate," he said, with a smile. "They've had enough for one evening I reckon." "Aye, but they'll be round early to-morrow morning, you may depend." "Most likely they will, and we shall be ready for them." Before sunset Endilloe had resumed its normal quiet, and there was no sign of any further hostilities. The family sat down to its evening meal in peace and laughed again and again over the events of the afternoon. Tom further enlivened. the proceedings by stories of his adventures in Africa, and little by little it leaked out that he had' flcsteturned to England a penniless lover, though, to v.i at extent fortune had smiled upon him he kept to himself. Justin suggested that they should get to bed early as they would' need to be stirring with the lark in the morning. Nathan was having supper in the kitchen with Amos Blue, who had pressed to be allowed to assist his master in defending his own. Suddenly Amos started and turned his head in a listening attitude. 7 "There's somebody a-prowlin' about at the back, Nathan, or I'm mistook," he said, under his breath. "Oh, it's the cows down in the paddock that you hear," Nathan said, knowingly. "No, it ain't no COWS; neither," Amos replied. doggedly. "There's people, or my ears be failin'.." Nathan paused in his eating and listened. "I b'leeve you be right, Amos," he said, with a look of concern in his eyes, and he stole across to the back stairs and ran nimbly up. The night was cloudy, and was, consequently, as dark as a June night could well be. The window of his own bedroom was slightly open. He crept stealthily towards it and listened. In a few moments he was convinced that a determined attack was to be made upon the house, but this time from the rear. Several men were moving quietly and stealthily about like spectres in the dim light. Nathan strained his eyes and fancied that he saw a big log of wood, which he had no doubt would be used as a ram against the back door.

"Blow 'em, they've choosed their time well," he said to himself. "They think we're oal off our guard or else that we're in bed asleep. How- somever, we'll .eoort let 'em knew that they're mistook," and he ran as nimbly down the stairs as lie had run up, and was soon knocking at the door of the living room. "Come in," was the quick response, and the next moment Nathan stood before them with a very white face. "What's up, Nathan.?" Justin asked, quickly. "They be at it again," was the reply, "and they're more ov 'ern this time." "No, surely ?" "As sure, sir, as I be a livin' man." Torn was out of the room like a shot. But it was no easy mater to direct a hose in the dark. Justin followed him, while John seized his double-barrelled gun which was loaded with peas and made his way to his own bedroom. Ile was not long in discovering what was up. It was clear that a simultaneous attack was to be made on the back and front of the house. Through the open window he saw four men creeping round the end of the house bearing a big log .of wood between them. He waited for them to get into position in front of the door. They stood close together, waiting probably for some signal. John was on his knees with the muzzle of his gun resting on the window-sill. His, finger trembled on the trigger. As yet no sound came from the back. He had better take the initiative; he could see the four heads bent towards each other. He pulled the trizzer. There was a flash--s yell as though all

the eats in St. lago had been suddenly let loose, and the four men cleared the garden fence in as manyl different directions. using language more lurid andj 13minne than had ever been heard in the peaceful itlehbourhood of Endilloe before. John withdrew his weapon and made for one of the back windows. But the report of his gun and the yell, that followed it had evidently frightened the besiegers. Ife was just in time to see a frenzied retreat over' the back wall, the pitiless hose drenching them to the skin as they made frantic and futile efforts to clear the fence at a bound.

But the troubles_ Of the 'besiegers were not at an end even then. On the other side of the fence were some forty or fifty men and lads who had come together in anticipation of further entertain- ment. These set upon the flying and drenched policemen and bailiffs and mauled them out of sheer mischief. If the first retreat of the evictors was ignominious, the second was even more so. They took to their heels in all directions and suffered many a scratch and bruise by attacking hedges and falling into pits, the dangers of which were not seen in the darkness.

On the following morning Mr. Bice was almost in despair. He might have the law on his side, but he had no power to enforce it. Policemen were few in that part of the country and they hated the task. Indeed, it seemed only too clear that all their sympathies were with the besieged farmer. Moreover, they found themselves derided on every hand. Mocking laughter and insulting words greeted them wherever they chewed their faces, and there could be no doubt that in any future attempt to evict the farmer they would have to fight their way through a hostile crowd before they reached the house at all. Mr. Bice discussed the matter with the Chief Constable from every point of view, and it was ultimately decided that the excitement must be allowed to die down before any further steps were taken. It was very humiliating no doubt, but in the present temper of the parish it was only too evident that any attempt to evict the farmer by force would lead to a very serious breach of the peace and probably to bloodshed. Indeed, so little did the constable like the whole business, and so much did he resent being a mere tool to do Lord Tregeagle's dirty work, that he advised Mr. Bice to accept his defeat and let John Pentyre remain at Endilloe on the old terms. But Mr. Bice swore that he would die first.

"Besides," said he, "I have let the house and farm to another tenant at thirty pounds a year more rent, and I'm bound to carry the thing through.' "You can better afford to lose thirty pounds than have the whole neighbourhood against you," was the reply. But the steward was obdurate. He had never been defea4ed yet, and he did not intend to be. "At any rate," said the constable, "you will have to make-believe that you are. For a. week at least you will have to lie Tpow. This ferment and. excitement will not die dow.n in a day."

"I know that," was the reply "and in the meantime we can be preparing our plans. There's no denying that we have 'bungled the thing— bungled it terribly. We must be careful not to make the same mistake again. Another such fiasco would ruin everyone of us." "It might ruin you," was the laconic reply; and then the discussion ended.
Meanwhile events were taking shape in another direction which were destined to .upset all previous conclusions.

div.head: CHAPTER XXIV. TOM MAKES A DISCOVERY.
div.p: CHAPTER XXIV. TOM MAKES A DISCOVERY.
°•Good lurks in unexpected places Waiting our need,"

The day after "the raid," as Tom called it, gave, promise of being just as tame as the previous one had been exciting. It was evident as the morning wore away, that the evictors were taking a rest. Not a single policeman shewed his face in the neigh- bourhood; though miners by the dozen we,re seen loitering about hoping for a continuance of the fun. John and his two men went out on the farm— that is, on John's small demesne of twenty acres which surrounded his house. Justin took further leave of absence from the mine, for his employers were in perfect sympathy with him, and told him that he could remain away as long as it was necessary for the defence of his home. Tom would have found time hang heavy on his hands only that Dorothy was constantly flitting about, and a smile from her every now and then quite. satisfied him.

So the morning wore away and afternoon came— sweet, dreamy, delicious afternoon, when all nature seemed to be at rest; when the very trees nodded in the warm June air and the flowers seemed to fall fast asleep. Tom and Dorothy found themselves seated in the window on the old oaken chest at the top of the tai rs.

Dorothy had been telling her lover of the fruit- less search they had made for the missing deeds, and how she had come across bundles of love- letters written by dead and gone ancestors and hidden away in a series of drawers that stretched across the end of the box. In describing these drawers she excited Tom's curiosity. "Were they secret drawers ? " he asked. "Oh, no, there is nothing secret about them,' "'Have you the key of the box ? " "Yes, would you like to look inside ?" "Very much." "I don't think I shall let you read any of the letters," she said, with a smile. "I don't think I want to," he answered; "but the old chest is evidently a curiosity." In a few minutes the lid was thrown back and the lovers were kneeling before it, Tom, with his trained mechanical eye, took in all the measure- ment& in a moment. .

"You are quite right, Dorothy," he said, "there is nothing secret about the drawers," and he pulled one of them clean out of its socket. He gave a low whistle as he did so, and then pulled out a second drawer and a third. "Why do you do that ? " Dorothy askedi glancing curiously at him. "I wanted to see if they were all of the same depth," he answered. "And are they ? " "I think so." "Then your curiosity is satisfied 7" "On the contrary, it is aroused." "Why, Toni ? and she looked eagerly into his eyes. For answer he took a small slide-rule from hie pocket—which a working engineer is rarely without —and began taking measurements. Dorothy watched him with intense interest and curiosity. "Well," she asked at length, "what have you discovered ?" "That there are three inches of space behind these drawers unaccounted for," he answered.

"You are certain ? " "Absolutely." "And what then ?" He shook his head and laughed. "Now you are getting beyond me, Dorothy," he said; "but we must discover if we can if there ts any means of getting at the back of these drawer." "You think there may be something there ? " "There may be. It was the custom in olden times before steel safes were invented to contrive all kinds of secret drawers and cabinets for the safe keeping of valuables." "Oh, yes, I know, and Justin examined this bbx very carefully to See if there was any false bottom In it." • "I don't think there is any false bottom,' he said; "but there is a false end, and the question now is how to get at it." For the next hour there was no love-making between them, which was rather remarkable • con- sidering they were left in undisturbed possession of ,the landing. Tom tried to put himself in the position of the man who constructed,the box. "He had to contrive a secret drawer behind those other drawers," he said to himself. "How would he do it?" As a mechanic he had to admit that there were several ways. "For instance," he said to himself, "he might - have. done it by—" and he leant forward and carefully examined the construction of the drawers; "but he didn't," he added. Ss by a process of elimination and examinations he reduced all possible methods to one. "These drat,ers come out en bloc," he said to Dorothy; "and there is only one way they can come out. You be how they are dove-tailed into the sides. Hence they must be lifted out." And he got on to his feet and made the attempt. Dorothy's face fell. There was not the least sign of movement. "I think you must be mistaken, Tom," she said, "they don't move a bit." "I hardly expected they would," he said, with a smile. "The man who contrived the thing would also contrive a means of keeping it firmly fixed in its place. That is what we have to find out." , "What you have to find out," she Said, laugh- ngly. "I am sure I have not one particle of Ingenuity in my nature."

"There will be a spring ot smile Other contriv. ance," he said, reflectively. "I mnst try to put myself in this old joiner's place again." Dorothy watched him with growing curiosity and admiration. The three long year that he had been away had changed him in nearly every respect. He was not less generous and light-hearted than in the old days, and yet there was a quiet gravity, an evidence of resource, 'a reserve of strength, a sug- • gestion of dignity that were altogether new. The youth had become a man. "There are three or four ways the thing may be done," he said, looking at Dorothy with a smile. "Let's try the most likely first." She did not reply, but she watched him as he pulled two of the drawers clean out of their sockets. Then he put his hand into the vacant space, and felt carefully along they side. - "Ali t" he said, with a little gasp, "it's very cleverly done. These old workmen were no bunglers. Now, Dorothy, we are all right," and in another moment he had slid oat the drawers and laid them on the floor."

"But there's nothing behind, Tom," Dorothy said, disappointedly. "You see, there's only that plain solid end of the box." "Looks like it, doesn't it?' he said, with s smile, "but that's where the ingenuity of the thing comes in. Now for another secret spring, and this- false end will come out." _ _ __ _
"But are you sure it's a false end?" "Quite sure, Dorothy, look at the thickness of the other end. Besides, listen," and he tapped it with his slide-rule.
- -- "It doesn't sound very solid, certainly," she

said. "I don't want to prise the thing open, if it can be avoided," he went on. "But if we can find no other way, we'll resort to extreme measures." "I'm sure you'll find out, if you'll do a little more considering,'" she said, with a laugh. "Here we are at last," he said, after a long interval of silence, "hut it's a tight fit:" A minute later and the secret recess was revealed.

"0 Tom," Dorothy gasped, and she fell on her knees again before the box. The recess was, full of papers, some of them marked by big blotches of sealing wax, others carefully tied with tape. "I believe we are on the right track at last, Dorothy," Tom said, excitedly. "These are evidently legal documents." "Let me go and call father and Justin," she said. springing to her feet. no, not yet," he said. "Let's not buoy them up with hopes that may end in disappoint- ment. We'll make an examination first." _

.. Dorothy knelt down again, and together they examined the papers one by one, Dorothy's-eyes growing wider and wider all the while. "You can call your father now," Tom said' at length, with a strange thrill in his voice. "By Heaven, we'll turn the tables on old Bice this time." But Dorothy was too impatient to go downstairs. "Father—Justin," she called quickly and excitedly, and her voice rang along the corridor and down the stairs clear as a bell.

"What is it ? " Justin called from below. "Come quickly," she cried.. "Tom has made • a discovery." Justin knew by the excited, tone of her voice something out of the common had happened, and he bounded up the stairs three steps at a time. "What!" he cried, as soon as he reached the top.. "Have you found the deeds ? " "Aye! They're all here," Tom said, quietly. Justin sat down on the floor looking very white, and looked at the papers one after the other, while Dorothy went off in search of her father. In the kitchen she came upon her mother, busy as usual. "0 mother," she exclaimed, "we've found the deeds at last." "No! " "As true as I'm living,. mother. Where's • father ? " "He was in the back yard a few minutes ago." ' Dorothy was out of the house in a moment. John was standing against a gate with his arm on the top rail, looking wistfully across the smiling landscape. The reaction had already begun to set in. He was fighting a losing battle, playing the part of an obstinate, unreflecting man. He was resisting, but resistance would cost him dearly in the end. What Mr. Bice had threatened might come true—he might find himself in Bodmin Gaol. Suddenly Dorothy's voice broke in upon his reflections.

"Father," she said, trying not to betray any emotion, "what do you think?" "Think, my child," he answered, slowly. "I think we are playing a losing game." "Do you?" she said, with, a smile. "Ah that's because you don't know. I've come to tell you that Tom has made a discovery." "What sort of discovery?" he asked. "Guess, father." "I cannot guess," he said;. moodily. "I'm in no humour for guessing." "Well, we've found that there was a secret recess in the old oaken chest. Tom made the dis- covery." "Yes ?" he questioned, excitedly. "And all the deeds were there, every one of them." • "No!" with a wondering look in his eyes. "As true as I'm here, father. What do you say SOW about playing a losing game?" But he did not stay to reply. He rushed past her with an alacrity he hadlnot shown for many a year, and was quickly by Justin's side looking- with eager and questioning. eyes at the heap of papers. For the next hour they sat around in various attitudes on the floor and on the stairs discussing the new turn of events and making a more minute examination of the papers. At length Justin rose tolls feet. "Look here," lie said. "I'm off to TrelfOrd." "What for?" his father asked. "To consult Lawyer Nankivel. There are a good many things in these papers I can't make out." "You'll not consult Nankivel with my consent," John answered. "Why not?" Justin, asked; in surprise. "Because he's hand' and' glove with old Bice. "Haven't you seen it- ?" Justin sat down, again. "You are quite right, father," he said at, length, "I can see it now that you have mentioned it." "Exactly. Now drive. over to Truro and bring back young Trendy with you. They tell me he's one of the smartest lawyers in the county. If the evictors turn up during your absence, we shall have an answer for. them. "They'll not turn up to-day," Justin answered, from half-way down the stairs, and a quarter of an hour later he was driving rapidly away in the. direction of Truro, When Justin had disappeared, John turned to: Tom and held out his hand. "My lad," he said, and his voice shook in spite of himself, "we owe all this to you and I'm grateful. I've not been quite fair to you in the past, I admit, but I hope you'll forgive me." Tom took his outstretched hand and grasped it in silence. "It was very clever of you," John went on, "very clever.. I never suspected a secret drawer, and I don't think my father did before me." "I should judge by the dates on the papers," Toni said, "that it has not been opened for nearly a hundred years." It was late in the evening when Lawyer Trendy returned with Justin, and he had made arrange- ments to stay for the night. It took hint several hours to go through all the documents, during which time every member of the family was on the qui vive. The lawyer looked up at length and said: "The estate in dispute is larger than I thought." is fully twenty acres," John replied. "It is nearer a hundred and twenty acres," was the answer. _ "That is what belonged to the Pemyres originally," John said. "It is what belongs to the Pentyres now." "But we've paid rent for it for the last, three generations, at least." "That may be. And most likely Lord Tregeagle will endeavour to make you pay rent for it still." "But you think the title is good P" "It seems to me to he without a flaw. Yet I have very little doubt Lord. Tregeagle will contest it. He's that sort of tarn." "Then how are we to act ?" "I should advise you to take the initiative and in bring the matter to a head at once. Tregearde's ,t,eward, I understand, has been trying to evict7you oy forcible means ?" 'He has." --Then issue a summons against him for trespass and for trying to break into your house. He will then have to shew his right, and the thing will ae put into train at once. I suppose you can find witness& who saw him here?" "Any number." Justin clapped his hands and laughed. *Glorious," he cried. "Evidently the fun is not all ended yet," and so it proved. But the fun was )f a very different kind.
(To be continued.)

Mr. Aked's Unpopularity. The meeting held in support of Lord Peel's report 011 temperance reform, in tee Parr Hall Warrington, on Monday evening was somewhat of a fiasco. The deputation which was advertised to speak did not put in an appearance and the circumstances lead- ing Up to this state of affairs were somewhat remarkable. Toe organizing committee at Man- cjiteter had arranged for a deputation consisting of ir W J Herschel, Bart., Mr J Herbert Roberts,M.P., and the Rev C F Aked, of Liverpool, to speak. Exception was taken in the town to the appearance af Mr. Aked on the platform, and as the result of an interview with the Rev F E Powell, chairman of the local committee, Mr. Aked decided that Under the circumstances it would be better not to attend. In consequence of Mr Powell's conduct the Manchester secretaries at the last moment Withdrew the two other speakers. The Mayor (Alderman Roberts) presided at the meeting, and was supported on the platform by the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis), the Revs John Tongs, F E Powell, J F Matthews, A M Mitchell, W A Knight, T Reed, and J S Hughes Alderman Monks. and Messrs R A Naylor, C E Parker, T Birchen, 8 B Stringer, R Wylllt, J Clegg, W Beswick, and H Taylor (police court missionary). THE MAYMI'S 111.1111CII. The Mayon announced that he had received letters of aPology from the Revs Canon Penrhyn, Pollock Hill. J navies C F Cross, T Pyin Williamson. T Bishop and C Hocken, and Messrs J U Hornell and C H Picot. The Whole of the gentlemen had expressed their sympathy With and approval of the object') of that meeting and re- gretted that they were unable to be present. Continu- l.ag.he said he was sorry to have to prepare the audience Eur a great and unexpected and bitter disappointment. Neither Sir W J Herschel nor Mr J H Roberts, M.P.. Would be with them, and it was perhaps necessary for blue very briefly to say a word or two explaining the Muse of their absenee. Mr Powell, the vicar of St. James', would explain ire more detail afterwards. He (the Mayor) understood that certain friends in the town !lad taken some slight exception as to the desirability of 'oe presence there of one of the gentlemen whose names Were mentioned on the Vecard as a speaker, and so huinerous were the representations that Mr Powell yteesidered it desirable to make the fact known e° this gentleman. Mr Powell was received, "1? the gentleman in a perfectly proper manner Who expressed no disapprobation of the fact that the knowledge was conveyed to him, and agreed that perhaps under the circumstances it would be b-tter for him not to attend. Unfortunately the knowledge of this fact Came to the gentlemen in Man- chester acting as honorary secretaries to this association, and they had taken upon themselyea, without knowiag the local circumstances, without being able to appreciate how far Mr. Powell's action was correct or otherwise, to withdraw the other speakers from the meeting entirely. (" Shame.") His own opinion was that if Mr. Powell bad acted with any indiscretion—he was expressing no opinion whatever upon his conduct except to say that he was quite certain he had only one motive in making the representation, and that was to do what be con- sidered best in regard to the cemmon interests they wore all trying to serve and to make the meeting as successful as possible—the matter ought certainly to have been "Ariel to him and the gentleman in question, but for these officials in Manchester to take up this matter with cettainlv an imperfect knowledge of all the facts and Punish them, and in fact—he said it advisedly—insult the PS "ple of Warrington and insult himself as repre- senting the people of Warrington by withdrawing the 'peahen' at the last moment and when it was too late tO rn.lte other arraneements to fill their places, was a Piece of unwarrantable conduct such as during all the 30 years of his public life was unexampled, (Hear, hear.) They knew perfectly well that upon the temper- ranee question or upon its social, moral and legal aspects ue had vary strong views, and he had net hesitated to .express them in very strong terms. He did, however, reel this—and he had felt it for some years—that if there had been a mistake made by the advanced or pro- gressive sestion'of the temperance party it had been in the direction of estranging those of more moderate views end compelling them to take sides against them instead uf being on their side in this big battle. (Hear, hear.) Twenty old years ago one of the finest pieces of initiate- Men as affecting the drirk question that was ever con- n'ise I was brought forward by Mr Bruce—(applause)— and if it bad become law the country to-day would not herrly have been better by millions and millions of pounds uut thousands of lives would have been saved and the !thole moral aspect and condition of life would have Peen almost indescribably better than it was. Haw was It that this proposed legislation never came into effect ? It was because of the indifference and apathy and to some extent active opposition of the temperance pert, theressioes. They did not want to repeat blunders of that kind. (Hear, hear.) They wanted to live to see some re- medial legislation in regard to the drink traffic. He was rapidly approaching the half century. and he confessed that it was with almost elokening dismay he looked upon one attempt after another which, because it did not g , far enough, was not accepted, and consequently came ono effect. To offer a starving matt a piece of bread was an act of charity,and he would be worse than a foal and an idiot not to accept it because he could not get a whole loaf. Starving men always did take what they could get. They were hungry far temperance leg- and,they would be worse than feces if they did nut take the simple modicum offered by one Govern- ment or another, and then having had their appetites hP' 'AA go for more and as often as they- could. telenlause.) He had explained to them their position. II was a little bit of an awkward position to be in, was it to ? (Laughter.) They bad, however, got the meetine, and they intended going through with it in Spite of the tact that they had not got a baronet and a m enber of Parliament and who, he was certain did not understand the oireumstances or they Would h tiro been present. Be was sorry to have had to Pteoere them for this disappointment. It was a bitter disappointment to him personally, because he thought the circurostanees which had led to the withdrawal of the two gentlemen were so insignificant as compered with the punishment dealt out that he was astonished that a min professing to have some knowledge of the guidance of nubile meetings should have actod In the way one of these honorary se,retarlea ha I done. The object of the meet. leg would be fully naderateed. Boras time ago a Royal C .mmlssion was apvinted,representing as it was th?oeht, all shades ot temperamse opinion and also the opt lion of these interested in the trade. The Commission sat, for a tremendously long time, and took an enormous amnesic ed evidence from all possible sources. The re- sult of these deliberations was that two reports were pres nted, one signed by a majority of the committee, and the other signed by the minority. If they took these tee) reports and compared them, thoueh they wle 1 of course end a very considerable difference b wen the recommendations of the majority and the min city, he thought they would be astonished, as he hat been, to find in what a large number of condition, the two reports abao utely or nearly agreed. He ven- tured to say at a meeting held in that hall twelve months ago :hat he would be perfectly satisaed,. for a few years at any rate, if the recommendations in the nniority report could only be carried into legishative off ict (Hear, hear). But the temperance opium IC the e sen•ry was so strong that it was considered cL"str- able thas, instead or suggesting the promotion of legisla- tion on tee lines of toe minority report the feeling of the entin.ry was stiong enough for them to demand that legi.lation should be given on the lines of the majority report. (Rm. hear),lllt was with the object ef supporting that position that this meeting Yam; hell. Resolutions dealing with that and the prevention of the elle of drink to children tied r sixteen years of age would be submitted. He hep,,d they would forgive him for saying that he did net rep ct a great amount of legislation in the direction of seced and moral amelioration from the preterit evernment. That was merely his own opinion and they would pr bably take it for what it was worth. At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, before Mr Birchall and other magistrates, Thomas leveled, a butcher carrying on busine,s in Crossley- street, was charged with haying been found in possession of the carcase of a cow, weigeing 445 lbs, which was unfit for human fod and which had been depositel at the Lower Seven Stars sleughter- house, Bridge-street, for the purpose of preparation for sale. He was farther charged with obstructing and impeding Ralph Norman and his assistant, Walter Flood, whilet they wet' carrying into execution the provisions of the Public Health Act of 1875. The rown Clerk, (Mr 3 Lyon Whittle) conducted the prosecution and the defendant was represented by Mr A Browne. The Town Clerk, in opening the case, said that for the first Gffence the defendant was liable to a fine of £2O or to imprisonment for not more than three months. Defendant had not been before the Court previously. On the 4:h of this month Inspector Flood visited the slaughter house attached to the" Lower Seven Stars" Inn, where by some arrangement with the licensee the defendant killed his cattle. The Inepeotor saw the carcase in question, and after eexsmininee it, informed Inspector Norman of bis opinion in the nutter. Inspector N 'mien went to the slaughter-honse at 7.30 and found the car- case of a cow. fhe internal organs were close to the carcase, which was dressed in the usual form for sale. He examined the internal organs, and found unmistakaule traces of tuberculosis. There were also traces of tuberculosis in the carcase. The pleura had bet fl remove° from the sides of the carcase—a very unusual thing in the preparation of beasts for sale. The Inspector called in the Derutv Medical Officer of Health, who at once came to the conclusion that the interuel organs were diseased, and that the disease was very clones developed. He advised Inspector Norman to re- move them to the Toe n Hall. With regard to the carcase Dr Gornell preferred to examine it by daylight, so it was left in the custody of Norman's assistant all night• Oa the following morning the deputy medical officer exam- ined it and founi unmistakable traces of tub.rculosis. The carcass was taken to the Town Hall and examined by a Justice of the Peace, who ordered its destruction. Inspector Norman grave evidence bearing out this etatement. With regard to the secnod charge he said the defendant kept " pestling himself in ha wave and his conduct was very objectionable. He refused to allow him (witness) to remove the internal organs unless he took the carcase as well. ?Fitness told him he would call in a pollee officer and with this object in view went to Market-gate. The d.fendant followed him, and during their absence the internal organs were removed to the Town Hall. Continuing witness said he made a search for the pleura which had been removed and eventually found it concealed in another part of the Cross-axamined by Mr Browns, witness agreed that it was impossible to tell that a cow had tuberculosis until it was cut open, unless it was in a very advanced stage. Everall did not dress the carcase ; the work was done by a man named etiredith. On a previous ec Mon de- fendant had sent for witness to -ee whether certain beef was fiZ; for food. Defendant had teem in business in Werrington for a great eucnoer of years and had never committed an off •cc- i of this character before. Dr Guest Gotnall, deputy Medical Officer of Reath, was then caled, and described in detail the coneition of the carease and internal organs. He was of opinion that the carcase was that of an animal which had been suffering from a protracted and severe emaciating disease. It was dark purple in colour and di 1 not "set" 5- mfg. Is reearded the internal organ.; he said that the condition of the lungs would be sufficient according to the recommendations of the Commission on Tuberculosis to condemn the wnole carcass. Mr Browne then addre,eed the Court for ths I defence. Us said it was a well known fact te,t lit was imp issible to tell when a cow was suffering from ltuberculosis until it was dressed, unless it was in the very late stages of the d sease. D ifendant bought the animal In coestiou from a most ra specta ble farmer It had a br itton hip ane Everali bought it for the purpose of dressir git and dispesing of it if it was fit for fond. If a cow te,tl a broken hip, no harm was done to th carcase. On the sit'rnoon in question defendant wet out, leaving instruccions for the carcass to be dressed He went out for the purees, of trying a horse at Stretton 'and he was thrown out of the trap. Hi ob. tamed something to allay his nerves—e(lau;hter)—and on arriving back at the slaughter h iu4e found Insp.ctor Norman there. Previaus to that time defend- ant had ney r seam the carcase, and he ('sir Browns) ventured to think that if be proved that the defeedant ' had not seen I, nut had left instructions for it to be dressed defendant could not be convicted. He did net, however, press the wile unduly against the defendant, et er the expls- li privately consider their decision, and cheirmal said they felt ii. div.head: USED WITH
div.p: USED WITH

IT is interestine and "The Balance of Trade." almost comical to see into what ecstasies a delusive phrase will sometimes throw a full-blooded p itriot. In the current number of the North American Review Mr Charles R FLINT has an exulting arti- cle on business prospects in the United States,full of patriotic elation of the most robust type. Eur- ope is alarmed, we are told, at American progress and prosperity, "nothing can impede or ston" American advance, and American prosperity is "built on lines that place us beyond the competi- tion of the world." Europe is bound to the United States. "We send them one hundred pounds of produce and they give us in return a few ounces of fizz and feathers. This gives us the control of the situation." Does it? is sure to be the kind of an- swer that will be given by nine readers out of ten. It will be cheerfully admitted that the output and exportation of American manufactures is increas- ing and is likely to increase. But that is not the whole of the case. The subject has to be examined in the light of true econcenic principles. Mr FLINT takes the exports of America and the imports, and he finds that the former exceed the latter. He calls this excess the " balance of trade" and the" surplus reserve." The two phrases are vague, delusive, and bewildering. What Mr. 'FLINT believes in, apparently, is that excess of ex- ' portation is wealth. We take his figures—and he carefully avoids details and tables—and they shew a balance of trade, he says, in favour of the United States of six hundred and forty-nine million dollars. How can that balance accrue? In what way does the money eventually pass into the pockets of American people? That is the inter- esting point. Great Britain,Garmany, and France have all "trade balances" against them for the ten months of -1900 which figure in his calcula- tions. Are these countries beirg slowly ruined P Are they, compared with the United States, less prosperous and less progressing? They ought to be, if his argument were sound; but, as a matter of fact, they are not, and so there must be some- thing wrong with his argument. Let us see what it is. The total trade of a eountry invariably tends to a balance of acrounts. The imports pay for tho exports, or otherwise there is never a settlement. For example, if the Ur ited States I' sends out six hundred and forty-nine million dollars' worth of produce more than it receives back, how is the excess paid for? That is the problem Mr. Furer leaves unsolved. The Ameri- cans never get paid at all, according to his own account of matters. The world owes the siX. hundred and forty-nine millions; and yet he takes the amount as something paid,and in favour' of the United States, when the trade figures shew nothing of the kind t In ordinary life, if a man's • outgoings are , more than his incomings, he does not reckon the excess of outgoings as profit, and. exult over them. The fact is that Mt FLINT does not understand that excess of exposts means busi- ness for which the imports are paying, and that the general account adjusts itself in this way. The true state of the account requirea detailed, state- ments, and not totals and phrases. This country may recive more manufacturea from ths United States than it sends in return, and if this were all, something else would have to pass to square the account, and the transaction would be simplified. But we receive back from thollaited Scats more than we send out, so that the balance of trade is ill our favour, arid not against, us. Wheat, gold and, agricultural produce are received by us, and they pay for our exports and cur investments. The United States are not doing well if their total ex- ports of all kinds exceed their imports of all kinds because they are not getting well paid for their exports. The fallacy is to assume that what is sent out represents money, and what comes back is not the payment for it. Moreover, British capital, invested in America, receives payments from American profits.
Agreements, secret The Tientsin railway aid" ing is only one of man"' and otherwise. . _

bad symptoms of Russian - Chinese manceuvring. We are quite unable to say into what entanglements we are being led' The Anglo-German Agreement as interpreted IV Germany and by our own Foreign Offiee,aa we bay° formerly pointed out, is not a secret documents'

and that makes a difference of interpretation the I raore extraordinary. COUNT VON BoLow said last week that the Agreement with England "has no reference to Manchnria." LORD CRANBORNE de- clared in the House of Commons on Tuesday that the agreement to preserve freedom of trade wher- ever the two Powers exercised any influence, to deny themselves the seeking of territorial advan- tages, and to maintain "undiminished the integ- rity of the Chinese Empire" was a provision "Without qualification." But COUNT TON BULOW further informed the Rarcasreo what was in the ruind of the German Government when the Agreement was concluded. It is worth while quoting the reference. "I can now add," he says, "that during the negotiations which lad to the conclusion of this Agreement we left no room for any doubt that we did not take it as applying to Manchuria." England thought Manchuria was Included, and so made the instrument appear as a triumph of skill and a declaration of policy. Ger- Many never intended to include Manchuria in it, and did its best to make that appear in the course of the negotiations, having probably agreed with Russia not to disturb her arrangements with China, in some secret fashion. Lord SALISBURY Would seem to have been misinformed and thoroughly outwitted. Again, on Tuesday Count I'ON BuLow declared that Germany had "no Political interests "in Manchuria. Whilst this conflict of opinion exists as to an open agreement, need we wonder that there is uneasiness respect- ing the series of secret agreements between Russia and China? That such a series exists there is every reason to believe, and that one of them was antecedent to the Russian occupation of Pert Arthur there can no longer be a doubt. How was it our secret service department was so ill- informed? We cannot say. Every step in China seems to bring us face to face with new secret agreements with Russia. The Tientsin dispute e,encerns a concession of land already conceded this country, and it has been cited as an in- artance of " Chinese duplicity." It may also be• 44 the other way. China gave to a British corn- Pans the the right of constructing a railway from vvehang. Russia now says that this conflicts With a previous agreement made between Russia and China, by which the Manchurian ra lway was to be Russian. A recent convention has been arranged between China and Russia, sad it con- tained provisions respecting Mongolia sad Tarkes- atan, giving Russia a virtual Protectorate. The clause has been struck out owing to the remon- strances of England, America, and Japan. Germany may have taken part in the pressure, but China does not include that country in her thanks, though Confir von BuLow did oe Tuusday refer to Important commercial interests Germany had In East Asia, which were directly concerned in eemg " that China trade does not become the ( t Y of a single Power or of several Powers." As 618 Manchuria is concerned, however, the new ve. nvention does give to Russia preferential min- !lig. railway, and commercial rights. British trade In the region may be almost regarded as *having eased to exist. It is time the secret agreements between Russia and China were disclosed. They are causing enormous trouble and constant fric- tlen• The Powers have convinced China, by com- Pelting modifications in the newest convention, that Russia cannot be permitted to have every- thing her own way, and China should now be Prevailed upon to produce all the Russian agree- °lents.

/I•The effect of the recent prolonged sittings of arnament is already beginning to tell upon the Naker, and there are some rumours that he con- 7emPlates resigning the office he has held for the last; seven years. These reports are an exaggera- 'iola of the fact, for although Mr Guey is sixty-six ' Yearsof age he is nearly as robust as a man in the ' Perna of life, and unless the exceptional strain is Prolonged far into the session will be able to rise tuperior to it. The out-and-out supporters of trade unionism, who have doubts whether eight i hours' work a day is not too much to impose on a British workman, will do well to observe some of Mr Gully's feats. On the occasion of the last : all night sitting he remained la the chair for a Period of fifteen hours, broken only by an ieterval tt'ef half-an-hodr for a chop. All this time he had ' maintain the keenest attention, the only IrBml really alert at several of the duller Stages of the controversy. Of course, during certahl parts of the session Mr. Gully receives sub- atenthil relief, for when the House goes into Com- mittee he is able to leave the chair, and Mr. )wther takes the reins. But even then Mr. peaker cannot quit the precincts of St. Stephen's, or if any disorder occurs it is his business to give a ruling upon it. The trouble of the whole matter ill that while presiding he has to follow the mist esearisome speeches as closely as if they were the most intere3ting, for only in that way can he pre- serve the House from irregularities. This sort of exercise, however, when the Irish are determined on prolonging debate is very trying, and if the Present state of things is to be continued Mr Golly will probably have to avail himself of the le-lp of the Deputy-Speaker for short Intervals. Tee werk nearly broke down the health of Lord Peel for a time; but Mr. Gully has not had his length of service, and the last thing he would con- template at present would be retiring. Lord Kitchener's appeal for winter comforts for . the troops in South Africa breaks rather unpleas- antly on the talk of peep), and the hope buoyed Up thereby of a speedy return of friends from the front. There is, however, no reason for depression Oil this aecount' or taking the notice as a sign that the euthoritiesbelieve that the war will be much 'oge • prolonged. Mr Brodrick has stated on T4'l4,ral occasions in the Commons the course whice ,t Lord Kitchener proposes to take. Whatever the LPlonatatic term used to describe the condition of i;u'ilre in S iuth Africa,it is certain we shall have to 4elz, e large portion of our army there for many ~."etos to come, over and above the increased per- -174,4nt establishment for which Mr Broderick has eetekoned. But, the War Secretary has also ex- e"eined, it is intended to relieve at the 11'1.1410st possible moment the troops who 'eve served so long, and the large reinforcements 110 V being sent out will be utilised for that pur- r"e• Teem has been a large amount of (Its- I l!Pom talent, alike among the troops and their 2,lencia at home, on account of the prolongation of 'it?e Campaign ; but the resources of the burghers e "ow pretty defiaitely gauged, and the convic- ee that the work of the military will Boon be ' 2ttln more than police worx is general. The Zeereah of winter is very trying to the men, who 0" been weakened by fever,and it is to be hoped tt the enthusiasm of the public will not slacken 't this time. The response should be quick and C4"nerons—not the less because the war has,in spite of the best efforts of the rank and file, become a tiresome affair, and involved ID many 'enues in gloom and mourning.

The appointment of porter and portress at the ;oiting of the Warrington Board of Guardians :44t we,-31r raised one of those thorny religious PICa Of which there seems to be no end. When 14adidate appeared before the Board he was ;I'll:stioned as to his religious belief. This r query query was too much for the Rev. J. H. "•!'idkitte, the ever-alert Guarlan horn Haydock vtgorously protested against any such cate- . 13Ing of candidates. The Ciiairman of the Board, l'vever, ruled that it was a legiti,nate qoestion and accordingly etton candtdate was , to state his religious belief. The t'ioct n,• view is not altogether clear.

A Workhouse porter's duties are not sup- posed to include those of a religious teacher. We can hardly conceive of such an officer address- ing the tramps on the preciousness of ieligion either orthodox or otherwise whilst distributing the meagre fare which the Guardians in their charity dispense to the poor vagrant in return for a few hour's stone-breaking or wood-chopping. It is therefore somewhat difficult to devise the meaning of the Guardians in attaching so much importance to the porter's religion. It cannot surely be attributed to a desire on the part of some members to exclude Roman Catholics from public offices. And yet some colour seems to be given to such a conclusion by the statement of one member that if a Roman Catholic were ap- pointed he might have to neglect his duties in order to attend mass. We hope for the credit of the Guardians there is no such predilection to act un- fairly to a candidate becalse of his religious belief.

The duties of borough auditors still remain legally undefined, the consequence being that each official acts according to his own interpretation of those dutiesit is still fresh in our recollection that this state of things led to a not very seemly dis- pute in Warrington, and the action of other authorities and officials in similar circumstances is thereforika matter of consi ierable interest locally. Darwen ' possesses an elective auditor who has a very lofty —perhaps exagg,erated —notion of his duties, and we can only surmise what would have been the extent of the explosion in War- rington had one of our auditors taken the course that Mr. Rawlinsonof Darwen has seen fit to take. This gentleman was only elected on March lst,but he has already tackled an influential and popular member of the Council, Mr. Brindle J.P., who has I recently become a director of a limited liability company which has for twenty years done busi- ness with the Corporation. The Councillor seems to have acted thoughtlessly, and though his posi- tion was legally unassailable, he has resigned in cons,quence of the action of the new elective auditor. The latter, after the manner of new brooms, seems to have swept clean. He took the drastic course of instructing a solicitor to send the Councillor an ultimatum which offered him the choice of resigning membership of the com- mittees trading with his firm, of resigning from the Council, or of severing his connection with the firm. Though the Council exonerated him from all blame, Mr. Brindle insisted upon resigning from the committees specified. Mr Rawlinson does not seem to have been content even with this for a further letter from his solicitor called upon the Councillor to retire from the Council, or he, the auditor, would not sign the accounts. Mr Brindle, who seems to have been very complaisant, therefore placed his resignation in the hands of the Council, by whom it will be considered at the next monthly meeting. That is the history of the afbir as it appears in the press. Though we sup- ported the Warrington auditors in the action they recently took, we should not go so far as to even attempt to justify the course taken by Mr Raw- linson of Darwen. There may be more in the case than meets the eye, but on prima facie evidence the auditor appears to have exceeded all bounds, either legal, moral, or courteous. We shall await the sequel with keen interest. caamax....4lo••••••

It is interesting, to say the least, to find bishops taking a practical interest in the licensing question- They appear to see the necessity of not attempting top much. The Licensing Sessi n Bill, of which the Bishop of Winchester moved the pecond teadi g in the House of Lords, is designed to give effect to certain recommendations which were summarised in identical terms by the majority and minority sections of the Royal Commission on liquor licensing laws. The Legislature were now simply asked to sanction changes upon which the whole of the commissioners were practically agreed IThe Bill provides that no person who would be dis- qualified by Section 60 of the Licensing Act of 1872 to act as a justice for any purpose under the ILicensing Acts in any dig rict should, as respects that district. he appointed to act as a member of the Watch Co ~mittee, or as clerk to the magis- trates Then the measure provides the t the anqual 1 licensing session shall be in March instead of Sep- temper as at pres nt, some of the temperance party being of olinion that there would be a better attendance of lice .sintt justices in Niarch than in the latter months. On th , whole, the mess .re appears a harmless on ,and eventual ly some of its prop )sals may be grafted on the more important Bill to be brought in by the Home secretary.

Anticipations of the Budget, " intelligent " and otherwise, continue to be exercised in mast parts of the country, and it cannot be correctly said that the Cha ,cellor of the Exchequer is the only one immediately affected by the prac ice, for it pro- duces a certain amount of depression in trade. As a certain large firm in the tea business have point- ed out, the immediate removal of duty-paid tea from the warehouse and the payment of duty ab- sorb so much capi al that buying for stock to retain in bond is necessa ily somewhat restricted, with consequent limited market competition. It has been rumoured in the highest busin es quarters that he amount to be raised by fresh duties will n4be so large as some people imagine. Instead , of imposing additional taxation to any great ex- , tent, so the report goes,the Chancellor of Exchequer I will act on the theory that some portion, at least, of the cost of the war, shall fall on the shoulders of fit ur g aerations, who will t)enefit to a greater extent than the present from the expansion of the Empire. If Sir Michael Hicks-Beach cares to pro- duce a popular buiget, this portion of the rumour will be not too good to be true, since it is what most people will be ready to approve. At the same time, with so large an amount of money to raise, it would he too much to expect that Sir Mi Ithael would leave taxation precis •ly where it is at pre- bent; and the mosl• that can be expected is hat any new taxes will be upon luxuries, and not the nec tasaries of life.

Th-i society has for its ohjiict the study of nature fto n the humanitarian rather than thi purely scientific side- While many of its members are naturalists of the hizhe.t attainments, it seeks to encou-age the preserva en of ran an beautiful forms of life, rather than to add to the collections of inanimat- objects whioh fil Museilnlll.
