all that is lovely and of good report, come within the scheme of the society's work. To such as love nature, for her own sweet sake,the society appeals, and if they are numerous enough in this town or the district to form a branch, the position of secre- tary should be welcome, inasmuch as it would bring them into touch with kindred spirits, and enable them to do much useful and pleasant work.

Local authorities and gas companies still contrive to have their little difference which seem to lead to any number of experiments in public lighting. Something of this kind has just happened at Latin- ces on. in Cornwall, where a portion of the town is about to be lighted, at auy rate temporarily, with acetylene gas, with the possibility that the whole of the streets may eventually be lighted in the same way, instead of by coal gas. The question at pre- , sent is, whether acstylene lighting can be effected as cheaply as lighting with the ordinary gas. The au.hority is not on the best of terms with the gas company there, but will not carry its objection the length of paying a much larger sum for public lighting, even though the light may prove to be of a superior quality. It has vet t) be shown whether the light would be much better, and meanwhile other email towns are look- ing on with the keenest interest, especially as there does not appear to be so immediate a prospect of lighting with electricity as had been previously ex- pected. Out of Launce Mon's difficulty other Cornish towns, and poisibly places beyond the county, are hoping to be profited, although as yet the experiment has not been made. It is in this way, however, that discoveries sometimes happen of the greatest value and importance.

div.head: RUNCORN BOATING CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN BOATING CLUB.

rne annual general meeting of the above-named club was held in the Brunner Guild Hall on Tues- day evening. There was a larger gathering of mem- bers than on any previous general meeting. Mr Buxton occupied the chair. Tbe first business was the secretary's (Mr W A Millinger's) report, whichlreads as follows :—" It gives me great pleasure to be able to report at this our seventh anuual meeting, that the progress of the Runcorn Boating Club during the past season has been as satisfactory as the most •sanguine and enthusiastic member could wish. 1930 hss been a better season in every way than 1899, just as 1899 was better than its predecessors. and I feel confident that the club will continue to enjoy increased pros- perity from year to year. During 1909 we admitted to the privileges of the club 39 new members, though of course we had some withdrawals of old members. Three have gone out to serve our country in South Africa. I refer to Mr Stanley Banks, Mr Tom Mellor, and Mr H Hill, and al:a sure we all wish them a safe return. One or two members, amongst whom are Mr J Speakman and Mr Percy Williams, have left the town, and 1 think lam merely voicing the eentimeet of this meeting in wishing them every success in their new spheres of labour. Again lam sorry to say death has been in our midst, and has taken away one of our most promising members, namely,Mr Allen,and I am sure the members were pleased to notice that the committee forwarded a floret tribute, with a letter of condolencs to his parents. at the time of interment Last season, owing to the kindness of Ar °timer, we were able to erect a small landing stage opposite the boat house which will soon save its cost in the saving of wear and tear to the boa s. Mr J W Wiewall must take credit for the design of the same. Three new boats have been added to our stock, with a seating capacity of at least eight, i.e., two boats of the" Sweetheart class, and one two-pair scull, inriggel The latter wig practically given to Us by Mr Whinyates, who sold it at a most reason- able price, and the that its of the club are hereby tendered to Mr Whinyates for his generosity in the matter. The races promoted last season I regret did not receive the support we hoped, and it is desirable that the members will show a more sportsmanlike spirt in the events brought forward by the com- mittee The dance held in December was not the suceess financially we had hoped it would be, but I socially I think it was a decided success. 1900 had seen us yeked with a Poor Rate assessel at £B, I which Mr Johnson has got re luced to £3 15s. Mr Mom a our care-taker bee been most indefatigable 1 in his efforts to keep the boats in good working order, and he must be complimented on having given great satisfaction to all in this direction. The Outgoing Committee taken as a body will want some beating, and I should like to voice the great satisfaction I have felt during the past year at the very hearty and attentive manner in which the club's business has been dealt with by them. As regards 1901, we have prospect so early of a very good run. To-night we have close on 20 new members for election. In conclusion, I most earnestly wish, as we all do, that the R. 8.11., will long confines to advance year by year as it has bean advancing since its inauguration in 1894. (Applatime)." Mr A Patin considered the report presented by the secretary a most excellent one, and he had mush plc 'sure in proposing its adoption. Mr Pea- cock seconded. The Treasurer, Mr H G Johnson, submitted hia crish report, which tell Tted great credit on his office. Us stated that although he had not bad the balance in hand he could boast of at the beginning et last season yet the turnover this year had been almost as big. The turnover was almost £7O, and out of this £4O, had been outlayerl on boats, an 1 cost of repsirs &c., to house and boats, while ! stationery, prostates, caretaker's salary, and sun- j dries, after being deducted still lest a small balance to carry over to 1901. He considered that the season had been a most successful one from a finan- cial point of view. He could endorse the Secretary's remark as to the progress of the Club, and also his wish as to its continued prosperity, (Applause) R Sherratt moved that the Treasurer's reoert be passed as read. He was pleased to have the msnattemant of the finance in such able hands as Mr Jeknson's.—Mr W Harvey sertended.• Mr 1:1 onnellan proposed that Lady members be admitted to the club, which was seconded by Mr R Sherrat. After a lengthy discussion the majority decided against the motion. Fifteen new members were elected. Mr P. Wright's proposed new rule to the effect that members be allowed to book boats for certain dates on paying a booxing fee of Say 64 each time, was not carried, as also was Mr vi, 1. Miningerte proposed new rule that all members subscriptions be paid each year at the commencemsnt of the season, and before tho clab's property was used by them. It WAS decided in respect to the latter to fix April 30th as the last date for payment of subscrip- tions. A rule to be numbered 24, "that the boat house be clo eel from January let to the last day in February I each year, and that during this time the b ,ata.be overhauled ready for the ensuing season," proposed by Mr W. A, Millinger, was carried with little oenositien. The election of officers was then proceeded with and resulted as follows :—PresideneSir R 14 ftooke, Bart ; vise presidents. Sir J T Brunner. Bart, ALP., Air C N Irven, Mrs Hazlehurst, Mr W Timmins Mr .1 II Baker, Mr J F Maslehurst, Mr R II Posner, Mr P E Sp nikman, J.P., Messrs Castner Kelner Alkali On., Limited, and Mr T N Smith •, secretery,Ar W A M.llinger; treasurer, Mr 11 (4 Johnson ; cantain,Air , F Abel.; stab-captain, Mr J W Wiewall; committee, Messrs G Buxom, R Bennion, R Johnson, W Har- vey. F Chrimes, A Donellan, F Mellor, and R Mid- field; auditors, Messrs It Bennion, and E Ward. ' A vote of thanks to the outgoing efficials, and 'leo one to the Chairman of the meeting terminated the proceedings.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

I learn that the Rtmcorn Football Club Committee have refused an offer of some .Cl2O, made by the York Club to :journey there to play off the next round of the cup. That the Committee have acted wisely and with true sportsmanship in such a mater is very commendable, for after all their first duty is to their players, and spectators. The latter especially claim inoulgence ; for, surely, afttr sup- portinp the club in season and out of season they are entitled to witness, whatever good items fall to the lot of the club, at the least possible inconveni- ence.

The injustice of forcing Nonconformist children into the Church and Roman Catholic Schools, is just at present being felt very keenly in Runcorn, and though parents are offered the so- called advantages of the "conscience clause" they feel that its acceptance is a worse evil than that their children should be taught dogma they do not believe in. As things are at present arranged the matter is very unsatisfactory; but, inasmuch as there are a number of church children in the Board School, could not some arrangement be come to whereby the dissatisfied ones could change places with the Church children; and in the meantime steps could be taken to so divide Granville-street school, that a choice of accommodation could be afforded all. Anyhow, it must be admirted, that some such course as indicated above would do much to eliminate the present cause for friction. On the other hand, if those church people whose children attend the Board Scbo)l do not see their way clear to assist in the arrangement, it must be because they think that Boar! School Education is better than that afforded in Voluntary Schools. And, if that is so, then the sooner the better we have Board Schools throughout the district.

Dr.Ludgwic Mond has recently discovered a cheap method of procuring gas suitable for heating and motive power, though unsuitable for lightiAg pur- poses. The gas. however, is of such remarkable cheapness that when used for the purpose of generating electricity the cost of drat beautiful illuminant will be as cheap, if not cheaper, than our present gas. Why I refer to this, is because the Runcorn Urban District Councd have already a provisional order for the supply of electricity, and it will pay them well to keep a sharp eye on the developments in connection with Dr. Mond's dis- covery.

" How a wilderness became a garden," would form a fitting title to the story Mr James Wilding (our district surveyor) could tell of bis work in con- verting Runcorn Reath and Common into the delightful sppt it gives evidences of eventually becoming. Few people, save those who have visited the spot, could adequately grasp the vast, improve- ment carried out there; and though far from com- plete, enough has already been accomplished to inr'icate that the grant of .£4,000 will prove meney well spent.

THE TRAGEDY Al ACTON BRIDGE. -Inquest and Verdict. Mr J. C. Bate, coroner, c inducted an inquiry at the Railway Hotel, Acton Bridge, on Saturday morning into the CirClinliqineSS attending the death of Harold William Livesey, whose dead body Was found on the London , and North-Western Railway, near A1..10n Bridge, on Thursday morning —Mr. John Triffitt, engineer in the employ of the Nth-Eastern Railway Cirnpany was present,whilst Ar. Bebbing,ton was foreman of toe jury. Frederick Livesey, residing at Bishsp Atli:land, identi- fied the body of the deceased as that of his brother. Efl was 34 years of age, and was a rail way engineer. He resided at Ben Rtiydding, Wiggington-read, Yerk. He last saw him alive in August. Witness knew he had been in ill-health for s sine time because his mother wrote hi in to this eft ct abut a fortnight age, when he came to Winnington to visit his broth, r-in-law. During the fortnight he returned once to Yoik. &reseed Richard Lucas, deposed that be resided at Winnington. The deceased Was nis broth-r-in-la w and had be sn saving with him for neatly a fortnight in con- sequence of ill-health. His medical adviser recommended him to take a ssa t.ip, ald ois Weckpsday iflarniag he left witness's residence arc smpassied by his sister for the purpose of catching the 12.10 train at Greenaiank for Liverpoal, his intention being to make arrangem eats for the sea voyage. He did nit return again, and that was the last time he saw him alive. The Coroner: Can you ;tolls any explanation as to how the sad accident might have happened ? Witness : All I can say is that probably he entered a late train at Liverpool, • hinking it w 'old travel to the station whence he started, but finding it stopped at Ac- ton Bridge, he thought he w suld wet* along the line. The Coroner to the Stationmaster: Could a man leave the platform and w ilk down the line without being noticed by the officials ? Tne Stationmaster : It could easily be done in the dark:

Edward Gerrard, p'atelayer in the employ of the Lon- don and No,th-Western Railway, stated tha- about 5.30 on Thursday morning he was walking along the liae near Acton Bridge Station, when he found the dead hody of a man lying in the s'x-f He had received injuries and wife quite cold. Witness simply examine I the body to ascertain if life was exinct. He then waked to di I nearest signal box, where ho teleph ric I for the station- master. The man was lying in the six foot with his head towards Gusenhank. Witness passed the spot the night before at 530 but never noticed anything on he bee. Two signalmen would alsi pass there between 930 and 10.15 the same night. PC. Wood said he received information of the affair lon Tnursday m >rning. Fl'A proceeded to the spot, and ' had the body removed. Od searching the clothing he found a rsilway privilege ticket from Manchester to Leeds. His watch, the glass of woich was brokon,was stopp.l at 3.35, but a watch maker informed witness that the works wete not brok9 en it having run d. wo. In his pockets was £5 in gold, 9.6 d in silver, and 51 in copper. Sergeant Griffildis : Wood lit not be possible for the driver of the eogine thar killed this unfortunate man to perc•ive that he bad run over something, and would not it be his duty to report so at the first station be stopped at? Witness replied that it was possible for the engine to have been jerke.4, btr no report bad been hande lin to that effect at Crewe. The Coroner disagreed with the opinion that the engine woad i hint Ele bad investigated several canes and neither the driver nor stoker had known they had run over anyone. The Coroner, reviewing the evidence said they could not corn, to a tt finite conclusion as to how the deceased met his death. The evidence simply showed that he bad been found killed on the railway They had not got the slightest evi-fence to show how he got there, an lit Was no use to consider the several ways in which the man C mid have met with his ,leath. The hero verdict to return would be an open one. verdict of " Found killed on the railway " was recorded.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

WEST BANE MISSION, WIDNES. There was a good attendance at the above mis- sion on Saturday evening, when an interesting tem- pera nce story was delivered by Captain Allen, entitled" Matt. Stubbs's Dream," illustrated with limelight views. Mr J Burgess superintended the limelight apparatus. UNITARIAN LECTURES. The Rev H D Roberts gave the third of the series of four Lectures on Wednesday at Runcorn. He said that whilst turning over in his mind the matter of the lecture " trnitaritteis and Jesus," he read the article "Jesus "in the new Encyclopaedia Biblica by the late Professor Bruce of the Free Church College, Glasgow. To his surprise it was just as he would put it himself, excepting that he could not quite leave the miracles where Dr Bruce did. This article by a great champion of orthodoxy was a significant sign of the times. HOPE HALL, RUNCORN. A pleasant evening was held in the above hall on Saturday last. Ur A Jones presided. The pro- gramme includA a recitation by Mr F Littler; solos by Mr Jr Findlow snd Miss Barnes; a dialogue by Misses Ethel Driale and Alice Orme ; mandoline silos by Miss Warburton; songs by Mrs Temperley, Messrs G Parr, A. Littler, Batt!eV, and Dabsen, and a duet by Messrs Gatley and Bettley The various Items were well rendered, and an enjoyable even- ing concluded with the National Anthem. ST. PAT/UCH's DAY IN THE DISTRICT, Seldom has the comcommemoration of this event been so marked in the district as it was on Sunday. Sprigs of "the dear little Shamrock " were very ex- tensively worn. At Widnes several of the trades- people had ordered the genuine article from Ireland and although the green was sold at high prices, this was soon cleared out, and the people then had recourse to pieces of green ribbon and clever. The commemoration of St Patrick's Day does not show the slightest sign of losing its popularity in the I chemical town. Runcorn was not one whit behind exemplifiedand n h especially, the Monday, the Irish element, as juveniles of the town, broke out in faction fights in the" rookery" and Mill-brow. No serious disturbances were, however, reported. RETIREMENT WITH RONOUR. Mr. JR Frith, manager of the Runcorn Gas Com- pany, on Monday evening presided over a convivial assembly of the employees of the Runcoro Gas Co. at Mr. Riley's Cafe, Bridge-street. The gathering i was n honour of Mr. William Travis, who for the last five and thirty years has been a pains- taking and steady workman in the employ of the company During the evening, Mr, J R Frith presented Mr Travis with a gold watch chain, and an inscriNed pendant upon which was the following :—" Presented to William Travis, by the employees of the Runcorn Gas Company on his retirement after 35 years of faithful service." Mr. Travis was also the recipient of a match box, a pipe and a supply of tobacco, which were handed him on the workmen's behalf by Messrs. H Chadwick and Turtnn, both:of whom referred eulogistically to Mr Travis. The latter very suitably responded. The evening's programme consisted of songs and musical interludes, and a very enjoyable tea. SONS OP TSMPERANCI9. A fraternal visit was made by the officers of the Weston divi- sion, Mr Jainss Cottersl ter* the chair, and was supported by the president, Mr Thomas Heeaena: At the outset Mr T Whyte congratulated Mr D Bis- brown on his recovery from a serious illness. Mr Daniel Bisbrown gave an address on Lord Peel's report on the Licensing fame, after having attended the conference at the Man- cheater Tows Hall. Before the magistrates at the Widnes Police Court on Thursday morning,Thomaa liarresonjohn-strest, Widnes, was charged with assaulting Winkel Atkinson, whilst psrformine his duty as linesman in the Salford v. Widnes match on February 23. The Widnes club Instructed 'dr Knowles to prosecute, taking this alternative in lieu of the suspension of the ground. Mr Knowles, in opening the case, said that Atkinson drew the referee's attention to some rough play. This irritated the rougher ele- ment of the crowd. AN INTERPLICADER CE.—lt will be remembe••ect that to this case, adjourned from the last court, Richard Collins, I plumber, of Runcorn, sued Mrs Henrietta Rushton, wife of William Rushton (in respect of her separate estate), for work done at 18. Church.street.—The case was originally heard and plaintiff Obtained judgment on the 20th Heeember last. When however, the bailiffs attempted execution the defend- ant's husband, William Hushton, laid claim to goods, and paid the disputed amount into court u ides. protest.—After hearing considerable evidence his Honour gave lodgment for claimant, each party to pay their own costs.

DISPUTE AMONGST Flid-DEALEBS.—Marg trot Carney, fish monger. Regent-street, sued George Low, fish hawker, of 7 Cooper-street, for £2 Ifs 3d. The dispute arose In connection with the supply of fish which the defendaist WAS hawking for plaint.ff. It was alleged that plaintiff had broken into defendant's stable and take t out his pony. Plaintiff, how- ever, pro7ed to the satisfAction of the judge that the pony was hers.—The claim was subsequently reduced to £2 8s 3d and judgment entered for plaintiff for that amount, at 109 a month.

BUILDING DISPUTE,—IGhn If Green, builder, Greenway- road, Runcorn. sued Samuel Cooper, Westfield-road,Runcorni for £l5 12s Id, for work done and materials supplied- occasioned by extra won( in the building of a house in West. field-road. Defendant filed a counter claim for £2 lie and paid £5 5s 8d into court. F A Lake solicitor, Runcorn, apueared for plaintiff, and Mr Joseph' Burton, solicitor, Rune irn for defendant.— From the evid- ence it appeared Green had contracted to build tha house for £lB9 and it was understood by both parties that the building should not cost more than £230 at the outside Extras were not mentioned, but when th- foundation came to be made it was found that an extra depth of 18 inches Was necessary, This and other extras conic ituted the basis of the claim —Mr. James Wilding (Bury yor to the Urban District Council) and Mr. J. Penniugton, builder, testified to the extra being essen- tial.—For the defence alr. S Cooper (the di-feudant) filizabeth Cooper (his wife) and Mr. William Farrell spoke of the understanding that no extras were to be included.—His Honour haring reduoed the claim by a small amount gave judgment for the balance 29195, together with the amount paid into court, for Mr. Green (the plalatift).—The counter- claim was non-suited,

On Friday Joseph Heyman, keiper of Old Croft Hall Wood, shot a full-grown fox with a fine brush in Travis's Wood, John Hayman is the keeper of Travis's Wood, and fur about twelve months the brothers have been endeavouring to trap or kill Master Reynard, who ha done considerable damage to the game in the neighbourhood, After many narrow escapes, a lucky shot brought him low, and the gamekeepers intend ti have him stuffed, so that a somewhat rare trophy will be preserved.

On the ground of the former. The visitors were the first to press, Callaghan being called upon to save. Williams made a good run, but was trought up in the nick of time. The B,4diers were several times penalized. but their defence was safe. Half-time :—St. Helens Rees, one; Orford Barracks, none. On resuming the vi,itors went away with a rush, Lawrence scoring. ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOUNDING AT EIAYDOCK. Patrick Rafferty of Efaydock, was charged at the Warrington Occasional Court on Monday, before Mr F A Frost, w.th unlawtu ly wounding Henry Smith, 10,Peel- street, Haydock, on Saturday night. The evidence was to the effect that on Saturday (St Patrick's eve),Rafferty quarrelled with Smith (his landlord), the cause of the quarrel being" E.gliohmeu v Irishmen." Smith made mune remark and Raff..rty picked up a jockey-bar, but dropping that seized a poker and struck Smith several times on the head, cutting the lobe of bis ear. Dr Henderson attended to the man's injuries. He was unable to appear at court, and the case was remanded or a week.
- _ A HEARTLESS Moraza. —ANOTHER SHOCKING CASE OF

NEGLECT. On Tuesday, at the Warrington Police Court, Jane Pool, was charged on a warract with neglecting her two ehildren in a raanntr likely to cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health.—Mr. A. Browne prosecu- ted on b-balf of the N.S P C.C., and stated that last week the Society Drought a case against a woman named Harrisen, who resided in Arkin-stieet„ When Inspector Hacktt visited the house be found the prisoner Poole lodging there. The house was in a shocking state, Dr. Bowden describing it as unfit for human habitatioa, and the Cnairman of the B nch remarking that it was not fit for a piz to live in. Prisoner told the Inspector that her husband bad deserted her and she had no inear.s of keeping the children except with what she earned by charring. The Inspector saw that th- children were in a dirty and neglected conditien and strongly advised the woman to. take them to the Workhouse if she could not keep them Prisnoer said she was going to live with her sister-in- law and the children would be properly looked after. Prisoner left the house and Inspector Hackett did no', see her again until the previous day, when be accident- ally came across her in a house in Leiceeter-street. He found that the boy Fred aged two and a half years, had two burn marks on the right band. One on the thumb was two inches long. Tnere was a very severe burn on the large toe of his right foot, the toe being almost parted in consequence of the wound. Be made inquiries from the prisoner's sisler-in-law and called in D. Bowden who said that the boy bad just been discovered in time. If the neglect bad continued, the probability was that the boy would have lost his toe altogether. Sant) E Poole, prisoner's sister-in-law gave evidence, She said the boy Fred was a "complete akeletorr. an i the baby was not much bet- ter. div.head: Warrington _Firm_ Sued at Birming-
div.p: Warrington _Firm_ Sued at Birming-
ham Assizes.

Before Mr Justice Phillimore and a special jury in the Nisi Prins Court at Birmingham AsAzei, on Saturday, the hearing of an action was commenced in which William John Churms,railway drayman, 157, Dial-lane, Hill Top, West Brom* ich, sought to obtain damages for personal injuries from trio defendants, John Buckley and Company, furniture removal contractors, Chnrch- street, Warrington —Mr AT Lawrence, E.G., and Mr R C E Plumptre (instructed by Messrs Willcock and Taylor! Wolverhampton)appeared for plaintiff, and Mr Hugo Young, K.C., and Mr W J Gandy (instructed by Mr A Browne, Warrington), defended. The case for the plaintiff was that on October last one of tbe defendants' vans loaded with furniture was sent from Warrington to Wednesbury London and North- Western Railway Station. Plaintiff, who was in the employment of the railway company, three days later tock the van out to deli eer the furniture. He let down a small tailboard or " cratch," and proceeded to unload the van. Whilst he was en&avouring to drag a safe oa to the tailboard it slipped off its " gudgeon " hinges and let him down. His arm was smashed, and hut to be amputated. He was thee incapacitated from following his occupation. His case was that the accident was due to the negligence of the defendants, in that their van was not properly fitted. It was contended that there should have been a nut cotter on the hinges to prevent the " cratch " from slipping. Mr Young, for the defence, denied negligence, and stated that be should call evidence to show that the tail- board was never intended to be used as a platform or " cratch " when unloading. It W6/4 not sufficiently sub- stantial for that work, and its attachment was such that anyone could see that it was unsafe. He therefore suggested contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff. It was further pointed out that the defendants were not responsible under their contract Co do more 'than deliver the van at Wednesday Station. After its arrival there their interest in it ceased. rhe managing director of the defendants' firm, Mr John Multett, supported the view that the tailboard was not intended to be used in the unloading of the van. It was very lightly built, and the chain which supported it was a very light one—a dog chain the witness de- ecribed it as. , William Henry Boote, Liverpool, said the board was intended to be moved away before heavy things were taken from the van. Joseph Muskett, coach builder, carrying on business near Warrington, said that the board was not a " cratch." It would have been stronger if it had been intended for use in unloading heavy goods.—The case was not concluded when the court rose. The hearing was resum-d on Monday when Mr Plumptre urged, that in the abaence of a notice of warn- ing it was natural and reasonable for plaietiff to think that ha could stand with safety on the tailboard. The jury found for the plaintiff, with damages £250.

A MAN wITH A eford, was charged I with being drunk and disorderly in Cooper-street.—He re- plied : I had some beer but was not disorderly."—The Magistrates Clerk: Then plead not guilty, if you are not gulLy of the whole.—The Chairman: You had beer. Did you know what you were doing ?—Defendant: No sir.—P.O. Gilpin stated he found defendant creating a disterbance in Cooper-street. He had run his wife out of the house with a knife a—Defendant dented this, saying he only hada knife in his hand to cut some tobacco with. —Fined 5s and 8s 6d costs. t DaMiar.—Jobn Flannigan, labourer. was fined 5s and 10: 6d costs, or seven days for being drunk and disorderly in Church-street. _ .

OBSCENE. LANGUAGE.—A WenslNG.—limanuel Carter, WSB given tha benefit of a douot about his having used ebseene language, wi;hin hearing of the public.—The Chairman, commenting generally upon such cases, said there appeared to be an impression abroad that people could give utterance to whatever they liked in their own houses. Such, however, was not the case. He took the opportunity of earning them that the County Council had passed a byelaw for public pro- tection, and wera determined to put down obscene an, pro- fane language, and inasmuch as there were children in alraciA every house,he thought their ears should be protected' " Fir TO POP THE QUESTION."—Thomas Farmer, a respectably dressed young maa from Widnes, pleaded guilty to being drunk and disorderly in High-street, Runcorn, on the 19th inst.—Constable Brett, who proved the case, said Farmer was going along the street singing " I'll be yonr sweetheart," and seeing a young lady in front, ran after her, shouting, " Will you ?—well marry me? "—Prisoner said that was not so.—The Chairman : You were not in a St con- dition to pop the question? (Laughter.)—Defendent, Oh yes, I was. (Increased laughter.)—Defendant added if he , had been granted thejprivilege of going home he would have. done so. He would take care it did not occur again,—Fined6s A RAGMAN CONVICTED OF THEFT.—John Critchley, rag and bone vendor of Runcorn pleaded guilty to stealing half- a-dozen sacks, valued about Is 6d the propert ; of William Worrell, on the 4th of March last. William Worrell, carter and:furniture remover. Vine street. swore he had stables ia Okeil-street. He used a large number of old sacks and wrappings in his occupation of furniture remover. On the 4th of March he went to St Helens to bring some furniture to Runcorn. Several of his swots got wet anal he left them in the cart shed to dry. The following morning he miseed them. Subsequently he saw Critoblev, who admitted he had taken them, and told him if be brought them back in the week he would say nothing more about them Prisoner did not comply and at the end of the week be toll the policv.— Albert Harri- son, assistant to Alfred Grounds, marine store dealer, Ash- ridge-street, deposed to the prisoner selling the sacks produced to his master for ltd.—Sergeant Gregory proved apprehension. On being charged prisoner admitted the offence. Subeiquently some 20 or 25 sacks had been recovered from the Marine Stores, and identified by Mr vVorrall as his. ---Prisoner elected to be summarily dealt with, and was sentenced to 21 days with hard labour.

div.head: MR. JOHN CROSFIELD'S GIFT OF HYACINTH BULBS.
div.p: MR. JOHN CROSFIELD'S GIFT OF HYACINTH BULBS.

The sixth annoal exhibition of Hyacinth Bulbs took place io the Lecture Room of the Warrington Museum on Saturday. As is now well known Mr John Crosfield of Walton Lea annually devotes a sum for the purchase of bulbs which are distributed tree to any applicant in the month of October and a competition takes place afterwards for prizes for the best blooms exhibited. Par- ticulars of the awards are given below. The bulbs to the number of 1,500 were given out in lots ot three (red, white, and blue) to each competitor, representing 500 households situate in the various wards of the County Borough: It is thus seen tkat advantage is taken of Mr Crosfield's generosity by a very representa- tive proportion of the inbabitants of the town—a much larger number of applications was made this year, and very many were disapoointed• The prizes are in them- selves vatuable and are intended to stimulate care and enthusiasm in the cultivation of flowers. The arrangements for distdbuting the bulbs as carried out by Mr Ryan are simplicity itself, and withal effected with very little expense ; Mr. Orosfield's gift being almost all devoted to the purchase of bulbs and prize,- money, the incidentals forming but a very small per- centage. After the judging was carried out, visitors were admitted and amen satisfaction could be heard on I all sides with the awards bestowed. The judging by Mr 1.1 Fulton Smith was carded out impartially, and this has proved a very important feature in all the compedtions extending over two years. One or two exhibitors pre- sented blooms which were raised from a different species of hyacinth to that given out at the distribution, and these were in consequence disqualified. The opinion of competent, practical gardeners testified to the careful- ness observed in awarding the prizes. The standard Of! quality in the present display was decidedly higher than in previous years, indicating greater appreciation and knowledge of the requirements of window gsrdening. Mentio: , may be made of an ingenious adaptation by an exhibitor of a wire-guard for supporting the plant while groaing—t e guard being held rigid to the edge of the glass. A number of handsome foliage plants obtained from the Parks Committee in the usual way were effec- tively arranged as a background for the better display of the blooms. Altogether a very pleasant afternoon! was aff,Tded the many visitors who availed themselves , of an opportunity to see the flowers.

INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARY.
Annual Meeting of
Governors.

At the Town Hall, Warrington, on Thursday last week, the annual meeting of governors of the Warrington Infirmary and Dispensary was held. Mr J C Parr presided, and amongst those present were the Revs Canon Willis, II V Pigot, E R Tar- buck, J Davies, E C E Carleton, Mrs Parr, Mrs Pickmere, Mrs Willis, Mrs Litton, Mrs C Jackson Holmes, Miss Massy, Major Buckton, Dr White, Dr Fox, Dr JosPph, Dr Richmond, Dr J Guest Gorn all Dr Battle, Councillors T Burtou and John Roberts, Messrs F Monks, John White, T Birchall, John Fairclough, C Jackson Holmes, G Thompson, El Thornton, E Pickavance, Joseph Taylor, with J L Tanstall, (hon secretary), and C Leigh (assistant secretary).

div.head: REPORT.
div.p: THE REPORT.

The Board of Management in presenting their report for the past year stated that the variations of income and expenditure as compared with the year 1899 showed that the income had increased by £36 123 41. The ordinary expenditure had increased by £24e sd. Both income and expenditure were, in the aggregate, much the same as in the preceding year. There was, however, a con- siderable reduction in the item "interest and divideeds on investments" This was mainly due to the sale of £6,780 Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway 3 per cent. debenture stock, on which about three months' I dividend had accrued, and to the non-receipt of accrued rents, not yet due, from the property adjoining the Infirmary buildings, purchased with the proceeds of sale of the stock referred to. The erection of a pathological laboratory bad been completed during the year, and the oast of the building and accessories had amounted to £297 153. This addi- tional equipment should prove of considerable advan- tage. The Beard regretted that the adverse balance on expenditure and income account had increased from £789 153 21 to £1,140 17 Bd,despite special efforts made by a committee appointed for the purpose, to increase the income of the institution. It was much to be re- gretted that the committee's efforts had not been more successful, which was, no doubt, due, in a large measure, to the many claims upon the public during the year for other deserving objects. The number of patients treated in the house had again increased, the average number of beds oocupied having been 31.65,and the average cost per bed £59 lie lid (exclusive of the cest of the new laboratory) as against £57 3s 9d in the preceding year. Out-patients and home patients had been charged against the account at the usual rates of is 61 and 43 per head respectively. A. legacy had been received from the executors of the late Mr John Hartley, and Mrs Eizabeth Hartley became allife Governor of the iutitution as one of the executors. Mr William Sloane also became a life governor in respect of a gift of £25. Ti. Board had to record with regret the death of edr William Mortimer, a trustee and life governor, and Mr John Edward Wright, who was also • life governor. SENIOR HOUSE SURGEON'S REPORT.

Dr BATTLE, in his report, states that during the year 1900, 624 patients were admitted to the Infirmary, 391 males, and 233 females. This shows an iecreaseof 63 patients over the number for the preceding year. Of these 504 were surgical cases; 120 medical. The acci- dents included amongst the surgical cases were 337,thus showing that the larger number of in-patients was due to an increased number of accident admissions. 36 deaths occurred lduring the year, 16 from accident, 20 from disease. The convalescent beds occupied during the year were distributed as follows ; Cheadle, 9 ; Southport Convalescent Hospital, 11 ; Southport Children's Sanatorium, 8 ; Buxton, 7 ; in all 35 bads, instead of 25 of the previous year. 1,096 new homeapatients were treated during the year. Tai s number shows a diminution as compared with the previous year which was consider ably above the average, owing to the epidemics of scarlet and typhoid fevers. The new out-patients numbered 2,477. 2,406 accident and emergency cases were treated during the year, thus makiog a total of 5979 patients treated at the dispensary. The PRESIDENT, in moving the adoption of the report and balance sheet, said the position of things was very much as usual and he hoped,satisfactory. He was glad to say that their institution had . fully maintained its position. The number of patients continued to increase so that the institution was doing good over a far wider range than hitherto, and they were jestified in saying that a great amount of suffering had been assuaged and mitigated, and in some instances where patients might have suffered total disablement had there been no such iastitution, they had been able to resume their normal occupation and continue to earn a livelihood. (Hear, hear.) It was a great satisfaction to them to feel that the institution was doing so much good and although the cost was considerable, still the expenses were not increasing to any startling amount. They world notice that the balance sheet showed a reduction of £75 in the amount treceiverfrom interest and divi- dends. The SeActary informed him that a portion of the £75 was due to the institution and would appear in the next account. They would remember that £6,780 worth of railway stock had to be sold in order to pur- ehase'some property in nose contiguity to the Infirmary. The committee, he thought,had acted wisely in securing this property, for although at the present moment they were not utilising any of it, in the course of a few years they might be under the necessity of doing so. The property, he understood, was giving them a little better return than the investment in railway stock, and they would always have it to fall back upon in case they required the site for extending the Infirmary. There was a slight increase In the cost per head, which Mr Tunstall explained to him as being in consequence of fewer out-patients. The debt of the inetitution, he regretted to say,had increased frees £789 to £1,140. This was to be explained in a i satisfactory way. During the year they spent £297 n the erection and equipment of a laboratory which might fairly have bean oonsidered as part of the capital account, whereas they bad paid it out of income. t!es believed they had got more than their money's worth in the new laboratory which would be of inealculatle benefit as their medical Men could testify. There was a trivial falling off in the contribution of the Workiegrcen's Committee. They all knew thew the working-classes had bean called upon to contribute ins great many other • directions during the year under notice, and therefore the result might be considered satisfactory. Next year they would have a substantial increase partly owing to the cycle parade held in September last. That would cone in next year's accounts. Mr MONKS seconded the adoption of the report and balance sheet and they were unanimously agreed tot

div.head: ROE. TIII&6171E11.
div.p: THE ROE. TIII&6171E11.

Mr CHARLES WHITS Moved the re-election of Mr Grorge Dakin as bon treasurer. Mr Dakin was at his post from week end to week end and he was sure they could not have had anyone better qualified to fulfil the office. A CAB DRIVER AND HIS SICK CLUB.

Claim at the County Court. Before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, B C.,at the Warrington:C'Ainty Court on Thursday last we k, Mannion a cab driver, who resides in Academy-street, claimed the sum of £6 5s from Edwin Plinston, 194.. Wilderspool-road,the secretary of the local branch of the Amalgamated Association of tramway, hackney carriage employes &c., which he alleged was due to him as sick pay."—Mr E A Connor represented the plaintiff, and Mr A Browne conducted the case for the defendant.

Mr Connor said the plaintiff had been a member of the Association from its inception until August last. When he claimed for certain sick pay he was refused on the around that he was in arrears to the amount of over 2s 6d, which would exclude him from the light of benefits. Plaintiff contended that he was not in arrears, and further th at if he!was, the local Secretary of the Asscciation did not inform him of the fact, which he was bound to do by one of the rules, before excluding him from benefit. A fortnight before he fell ill the plaintiff asked Mr Plinston how he stood in case he became ill, and defendant expressly told him he was all right. Mr Browne pointed out that in rule 39 of the associa- tion it was laid down that any member having a com- plaint against an officer or member &c., might appeal to the committee of his branch. In rule 47 it was stated that in no ca se would benefits be allowed to members unless they conformed to the rules and no excuse would he entertained by the committee. The defendant could prove that plaintiff was eight weeks in arrear. Plaintiff gave evidence and stated that he was 43 in arrear on April 11th, 1899, when he entered the employ of the Warrington Carriage Company. He paid some- thing extra each week, until the amount WAS paid off. At this point Mr Browne called attention to the fact, that according to a rule of the association, the General Secretary was the only person who could be sued. The claim was amended to that effect. Continuing his evidence, the plaintiff said he paid a contribution to Mr Plinston in July, 1900, a fortnight before he became ill, and he was then told that he was on the right side, as regarded his payments. In answer to Mr Browne, plaintiff said he had not paid anything since his illness and Mr Plinston gave him notice that he was excluded from benefit. He worked eight weeks at Messrs Richmond's,and during that time he paid subscriptions to the association tf ough not every week. Questioned by Mr Connor witness said that whilst be was at Richmond's, helmet with an accident and was " on the club" for a short time. For the defence, Mr Plinston gave evidence. He said that when plaintiff was taken ill he was eight weeks in prrear—a statement which was proved by the books of the Society. If he had paid the man anything under these circumstances he would have been surcharged the amount. Plaintiff never asked to go before the committee With reference to his meeting with the plaintiff in July, he told him that he thought be was just on the right side, but he was not certain.

His Honour decided that the plaintiff was in arrear He thought the man had been badly treated,but be could not see why he did not appeal to the Committee. He• gave judgment for the defendant without costs.

div.head: 3tettins to tbe etlitor.
div.p: 3tettins to tbe etlitor.

Warrington Guardians and the Religion of Officials. Bir,—l have read the account in your issue of last Saturday of the recent incident at the meeting ot the Board oi Guardians when candidates for the post of porter and portress at the Workhouse were questioned as to their religion. My friend, the Rev Jl3 Riddette, deserves the thanks of all Free Churchmen for his alert- ness in noticing and protesting against that proceeding. At this time of day,we do not expect, and cannot allow, that candidates for public service should be questioned as to their religious denomination. All public positions should be equally open to any and all candidates who have the necessary qualifications and whose trustworthi- ness, sobriety, and respectability can be properly testi- fied, It matters absolutely nothing to the Board of Guardians,or to the ratepayers whom they sometimes seem forgetful that they represent, whether a candi- date for office in the Workhouse, male or female, be Protestant or Catholic, Church of England or Noncon- formist. All enquiries on these points are utterly beside the mark, and beyond the province of any one to in- stitute. Here I venture respectfully but entirely to differ from the Chairman of the Board, and all others who on this point agree with him. In most matters, the Chairman's discharge of his difficult and onerous duties deserves all admiration. But on this point, if I may be allowed to say so, he did not display his usual breadth of view and soundness of judgment. Guardians of course have their strong religious preferences, or even it may be prejudices. But as representatives of a com- munity that includes all kinds of religious professions, and even many persons who rank themselves under no ecclesiastical banner at all, the Guardians are not justified in allowing their personal ecclesiastical prefer- ences to favour or disfavour any otherwise entirely eligible candidate for office. The chairman said that Mr Davies question as to whether one of the candidates was a member of the Cherch of England was a "legi- timate question." I deny that position utterly. And I wonder at a Nonconformist like Mr Thornton deeming a protest against such an opinion a waste of time! No one can wish the valuable time of gentlemen who so un- selfishly serve the community to be needlessly consumed. But when the question of religious freedom is in danger of being slighted and ignored, it becomes needful to occupy time in serious and earnest protest. I hope the Nonconformists of this district will make it clearly understood that they are awake to the fact that even in these advanced days there are not wanting men who will, if they can, make Nuitconformity a disqualifica- tion for public service, These gentlemen, some of whom are very unwilling to go to Church less they elated be , "preached at," will need to be prudently careful in their public actions, or they must endure being coun- selled as to their public duty. My personal desire and effort have consistently been to live and work amicably and peaceably with all who will permit me that pleasure I but this is an occasion when respectful ,but plain speech has become matter of paramount duty. Let public authorities institute the fullest enquiry into the probity, and capacity, and sober habits of every candidate far office. Careful enquiry into the latter eewicially would save many a subsequent difficulty. But beyond these reasonable and necessary enquiries there is no occasion to go, and into the question of a candidate's religious denomination, no public authority has any right to go! I sincerely hope that upon reflection even Mr A J Jolley will concede this point. The days of religious tests are over, and all lovers of religious liberty must see to it that no reactionary influences can succeed in bringing them back again. Yours faithfully, JOHN YONGE. 19, Wilson Pattenditreet, March 20th, 1901.

div.head: LICENSING CASE AT RUNCORN. – Mr. Knowles and the Bench.
div.p: LICENSING CASE AT RUNCORN. - Mr. Knowles and the Bench.

Warrington Police Force Inspected. Sir Herbert Croft, Government Inspector of Con- stabulary, made his annual inspection of the War- rington Police Force on Monday. The men paraded at the Drill Hall shortly before eleven o'clock. There were present the Chief Constable, three in- epectors,five sergeants, 40 police constables and two detectives. The men were put through their drill by the Chief Constable, and the various movements were faultleciQly carried out. After the inspection Sir Herbert Croft visited the new police buildings and then went on to the Police Station. where he inspected nine other members of the force, went through the buildings, and examined the office books.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, befere Messrs. W. Handley and James Pritchard, Mrs Alfred Taylor, licensee of the " Wheateheaf " Inn, Bridge-street, was charged with supplying drink to a drunken person, Michael Dowd, an Irish labourer.—Mr A Fletcher, Northwich, prosecuted for the police, and Mr J W Knowles, Widnes, defended. Mr. Fletcher. in opening his case, described Dowd's condition when taken in hand by the police, as literally poisoned by alcohol. P.C. Gregory gave evidence that at 10 o'clock on the sight of the first instant, he saw Dowd ejected from the " VVleeatsheaf "by a man name I James Ellams. Dowd fell to the ground, and was in such a helpless state of drunkenness that witness and Constables Carrington and Bowyer carried him to the Police Station. He .was placed on a bed in No. 1 cell, but fell to the floor and injured his head. Mrs Taylor when questioned by P.C. Gregory said that Dowd had been in hr house half an hour, and bad only had one pint of beer. He asked for another but she refused him.—ln cross-examination witness said Mrs Taylor was a widow. He husband was a noted footballer, who unfortunately was drowned in the river Dee in June last. Michael David, denied knowledge of ever having entered the Wbeatsheat Inn. The last place he remem- bered going to was a public-house in Halcon-road,where he was served with a "rum hot." Subsequent to that he remembered coming to in the Police cell. John Gregson, captain of the ship canal dredeer "Ark." testified to being in the Wheatsheaf from 8.30 to 9.30 on the night in question. He remembered Michael Dowd coming to the house, about 8.30. To I witness he appeared perfectly sober, and was supplied with a pint of ale. Later Dowd entered into an argil. merit with Gregson, and Gregson called for a drink for him. Mrs Taylor, however, refused to serve him, and later be was ejected by a man named Ellams. Mr Knowles, for the defence, argued that the balance of the evidence for the prosecution was really against themselves, and the case ought to be dismissed, other- , wise it would only necessitate an appeal. The Chairman : Do you put that as a threat ? Mr Knowles : 0 no, sir, I do not know, but that threatening maelstrates is an offence ? (Laughter.) Mrs Mary Taylor submitted that when she served Dowd, he appeared perfectly aober. She asked Mains to eject him because she thought there would be a bother when be began to interfere with Gregson. The drink he had in her house wouid not have accounted for Dowd's condition.—James Ellams, bricklayer, Runcorn, also testified to Dowd coming in apparently sober, and being served with a pint of beer. Witness was having an argument with Gregson, and Dowd interferred. He used very extraordinary language. Subsequently Mrs Taylor asked him to eject Dowd and he did so. Dowd appeared perfectly sober. After a very lengthy retirement, the Bench intimated they had given very careful consideration to the case and ordered that Mrs Taylor pay the costs.—The licence would not be endorsed.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
The Yarmouth Murder,
Execution of Bennett.

Herbert John Bennett on Thursdry morning suffered the law's penalty for the brutal murder of his wife on Yarmouth beach last September. He was banged at Norwich Prison at nine o'clock. Bennett proved an inveterate smoker, and has been freely supplied with cigarettes, The prison authorities are reticent as to his conduct. There ie reason to believe he has been left severely to him- self, and has received no visits from relatives or others.

Billington and his son were the executioners, and carried out the duties speedily. Bennett was pale and faint, and the body twitched violently for two minutes after the fall. The morning waa bitterly cold.

div.head: Anglo-Russian Dispute
div.p: The Anglo-Russian Dispute

Lord Lansdowne.

In the House of Lurds, yesterday afternoon, Lord Lansdowne stated that Russia and England bad agreed to withdraw troops from the disputed terri- tory and to reserve the question of title and pro- prietary rights for subsequent examination.

div.head: Warrington Volunteers for the Front.
div.p: Warrington Volunteers for the Front.
Interesting Presentations,

On Mon.l ay evening— an interesting gathering took place in St. Clement's Mission S -hoolronm, when the members of the Young Men's Bible Class aeeembled for the purpose 'of making a preeentation to Private T W Davies,one of the volunteer active service company now quartered in Orford Barracks. There was a large mad- tier of members and friends preeent, including the Rev A S Cameron, Mrs Cameron, Miss Gornall (the class teacher), and Miss Taylor, who kindly assisted in the catering. At intervals games and dancing were in dulged 'in, songs were renderel by "Miss Taylor, the Rev A S Cameron, Mr W Gregory, and Mr C J Sheath. and Miss M Boardman contribotel a recitation. The Rev A 9 Cameron made the presentation, which took the form of a Bible, wri'ing materials, and a box of cigarettes, ana Private Davies suitibly responded. An adjournment was then made to the side room for refresh- mente, which were under the charge of Misses Gornall and Taylor, who carried out their work splendidly. The 1 Proceedings terminated by the singing of " Auld lang syne " and " qod save the Ring.” At the Marvis of Granby lan, on Saturday night, a presentation was made to Private M Foster, one of the Warrington volunteers who has been accepted for service in South Africa. Private Foster has been employed in the netting department of Messrs Rylands Brothers for some time, and his fellow workmen decided to make the occasion one of enjoyment. Several employes were pre- sent, anA a very substantial repast was served by Hostess Whittle and her assistants, the subsequent pro- ceedings being presided over by Mr W Nield. Prior to making the presentation, the Chairman gave an interest- ing address on the sehject of the aear and the happy out- look of a possible early termination. The preeencation, which took the form of a handsome sum of money, wag then made, the recipient suitably responding. A capital programme of music was afterwards gone through, the accompanist being Mr Bert Smith. Abeut 24 members of St Like's Young Men's Recrea- tion Club met in the schoolroom on Monday evening, to present Private Woodhead, a member of the club, with smoker's materials and writing outfit, on his going to the front. About eight o'clock all sat down to refresh- ments,after which the Rev HR Wilda made the presenta- tion, in a few suitable remarks. The rest of the eveeine was spent in a convivial manner, songs being rendered by the following :—Messrs T Ashcroft, " Hearts of Oak "; J Woodhead," It's hard to say goodbye" J Lightfont, "Ordered to the Fray " ; T Ashcroft, "The Old Folks at borne" ; and J Woodhead "Queen of the Earth." A pleasant evening was brought to a close by the singing of "Auld lang syne" and the National Anthem.

div.head: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER CONCERT.
div.p: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER CONCERT.
Visit of the Royal Welsh Ladies Choir.

A concert with the very worthy object of promoting the fund for the re-inuring of the lives of the Runcorn Volunteers now fighting at the front, and for insuring the lives of those about to go out, was on Friday last given at the Drill Hall, Runcorn. The artistes were the Royal Welsh Ladies' Choir (conducted by Madame Clara Novell° Davies) ; with Miss Marie Novelle Williams, (pianist) ; and Mist Backsheen Wood (solo violinist). The choir has already attained a world-wide reputation, and to attempt to add anything to its laurels would be indeed difficult. However, it was its first visit to Run- corn, and therein lay the novelty. A fair audience assembled and listened attentively to a performance which was a treat. The choir gave " Role Britannia." " Spanish Gipsy " (competitive piece at Chicago), "Fair Land we Greet Thee," " Ash Grove." " Day is at last departine."and an arrangement of "Welsh Airs." " Sands of Dee," by Miss Hannah Whitman,and "Abide with me." by Miss Mary Powell were very effective. Miss Maggie Sambrook was responsible for a delightful conception of " Kathleen Mavourneen." Two violin solos by Miss Backsheen Wood, " Fantasie Brillant "and " Ungarische Rhapsodie," in- indicatad a remarkable memory and a capab'e control of the instrument, the harm.nic notes being exceptionally clear and sustained. Both items were deservedly en- cored. The item of the evening, however, was Mies Marie Novelle Williams' interpretation of Liszt's delight- ful pianoforte solo " La Campanella," which was given in a manner that brought down the houae:An cncore was undeniable. Miss Mary Thomas and Miss Mary Jenkins as principals in " Misereri " (11 Trovatore) exhibited extraordinary vocal powers. Miss Jenkins proving a remarkably fine tenor. " Love the pedlar," was given by Miss Maggie Lewis ; " 0 that summer smiled for aye," by Miss Gertrude Wedlake ; " For all eternity,"by Miss Bessie Woodward: whilst Miss Annie Ball exhibited a phenominal voice in "Poor wandering one" and "Spring is coming! Miss Mary Jenkins then further captivated the audience with " The old Plaid Shawl" and had to respond. By request the choir added "March the men of Harlech," and tbe whole concluded with " God save the King."—The concert was an im- mense musical success, and once again the Runcorn public are indebted to Captain Ashton for the treat of the season.

div.head: Warrington County Petty Sessions
div.p: Warrington County Petty Sessions

WEDNESDAY—Before Captain Withington (in the chair) and Mr John White. Coir. mancrumsys FlNED—Messrs Richard Evans and Co., coal merchants and colliery proprietors, were summoned for allowing a vehicle which had not the tare weight marked upon it to be used for the delivery of coal at Poulton on the 7th Inst.—P.B. Brindle said that on the afternoon of the date mentioned he saw one of the defendants' vehicles in Warring- ton-road. Poulton. The cart was laden with coal, which, was afterwards delivered at the Union Schools. Padgate The tare weight was not marked on the cart. The No 153 was chalked on the back.—Mr London. I he firm's Warrington agent said the plates showing the tare weight were detachable and must have fallen from the cart before it left the yard.— A fine of 5e was imposed. THE EXAMINER FRIT4AY, MARCH 22 1901.
EARLESTOWN & NEWTONST PATRICK'S DAY CELEBRATION 1 AT EARLESTOWN.
TEMPORARY AUTHORITY.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes lay, before Captain Withington and Mr John White, Thomas Fairhurst was granted tem- porary authority to sell in lieu of Joseph Goulden at the Railway Hotel, Golborne. P.S.A.

The usual weekly meeting of the Barlestown and I District P.S.A. Society, was managed by ladieP. Mrs George presided, and there was a large number pre- sent. Vecal items were given by Mrs Ormand, and recitations by Mrs Valentine,who also accompanied on the piano. Mrs Burgess gave an interesting ad- dress on theeory of ' Martha and Marv." DEATFL OF MRS. J. FITZGERAL,.

Much surprise was evinced in Ear, gtown on Wednesday morning by the announcem.- t of the sudden death of Mrs Fitzgerald, wife of Councillor John Fitzgerald. The deceased lady appeared to be in good health and spirits up to retiring to bed on Tuesday night, hut at four o'clock on Wednesday she was dead. Shortly before that time she was delivered of a c'aild,and although Dr Mouncey was in immediate attendance, he was unable to arrest the rapid sinking which ensued. Much sympathy is felt with Councillor Fitzgerald who is left with four children.

Irish M.P's Speak Out Strongly. The Earlestown branch of the United Irish League of Great Britain celebrated the day of their patron saint by a concert and meeting in the Town Flail, Earlestown on Saturday evening. The ball was crowded to excess by a Most enthusiastic audience who applauded loudly the Various items submitted by an excellent array of artistes including Miss Dorothy Kilby, Miss Nellie Fisher, Mr R Kay, Mr C Nary, and Mr W Touleon all of Liverpool. The Earlestown Oechestral Band was also present, and submitted a couple of selections under the conductor- ship of Mr Ashley. Alter the conc-rt a meetiug was held under the chairmanship of De P F O'Keifie of St Helens who was supported by Mr Field, M.P., Mr Alder- man Joyce, M.P., and Mr O'Donnell, M.P., who gained notoriety by addressing the speaker of the Hon.° of Commons in Irish. A number of local members of the League were also on the platform, 111 r John Dillon, M.P. for East Mayo should have been present, but the chair- man regretted to have to announce his inability to be presenr in consequence of a severe illness. It was a great privilege to an Irishman to be present to see such a grand assembly of Irish ladies and gentlemen. Be was sure the committee had to contend with a combined force of enemies, political or otherwise. Be , was very proud to bear that they had in Earlestown clerical influence at their back. In some of che other towns they were harrassed by clerical interest. There were as fine men in their churches from the Irish ranks as existed through the whole world, as able and enthu• Mastic in the welfare of their country as they could get in the ranks of the Irish Parliament party, but unfor- tunately on the otherlhand clerical influence had worked aeainst the United Irish League. In their ranks they must admit, there was some who, in various times and in divers eases had proved to be anything bu ; Loyal Irishmen, but, on the other hand the members of the League had proved beyond yea or nay that they were staunch thorough-going Irishmen. (Hear, hear.) He must say in reading over the various histories of old ' Ireland that some of the clergymen of the Catholic Church did not impress him very favourably, some of them had the interest of the country at heart as much as the Church which bad called them, but on the other hand some were influenced by statements which had reached them, statements not based upon straight- forward grounds. They had present that night men who . were present when the evictions took place in the House , of Commons. (Applause.) They bad °resent more than one of those whom it took 19 stalwart London police- ' men to shift. With snob men, so capable, so energetic, so enthusiastic, so bound up in the welfare of their , country, who took part in the mortal fight in the House of Commons, when some of their English M. P.'s tried to • vote 17 millions more money out of the pockets of the , workingmen, and yet Beene people who were in the

_— House of Commons would have voted this money away without debate, were it not for such fine stalwart,able fiehting men as they had there that night (Cheers.) Mr.M. Flannagan said the Irish cause was no trumped up Cause, it was a noble, honest, Leer, cause, a cause that no man whether he was Irish, English, Scotch or Welsh need be ashamed of falling, in wit,] and working for. He moved "We express our sincere sorrow at the inability of Mr John Dillon to beepresent at the demons- tration to-night, and we fervently hope that he will soon be better to once more resume his work for the cause of Ireland's liberty ; that we pledge our firm adhereace to the principles and oojects of the United Irish League a, established by the convention of the Irish race, and that we take this opportunity of renewing our con- fidence in the Irish party led by Mr Redmond,and hereby pledge'our hearty co-operation and support."(Appleuse.) .—M: L Murphy seconded. Mr W Field, M.P., speaking in support, said they were there that night in the heart of E igland carrying on the struggle for the emancipation, and for the freedom of Ireland. Ireland had never been conquered and never would be conquered. (Cheers.) The spirit of their race had carried on this long struggle through ages which had been sanctified through the pages of history. The Irish party in the House of Commons was now the only party which represented the people. What was the House of Commons to-day ? It was a club of rich men, a rich man's debating club ; it was a machine for taxa- tion, for free speech was denies!, it was a mere instrument in the hands of a Government under the name of a constitutional rule which absolutely denied to a majority of the people's representatives any oppor- tunity of bringing forth those measures which were demanded by the constituencies of Great Britain and Ireland. No private member had any opportunity of , bringing in a measure which would be useful to his con- ' stituents or the people at large. What bad become of the Old Age Pensions? What had become of the Housing of the Workers? What had b.come of all those great measures which had been promised by Conservatives when they sought the votes of the electors at the time ef tbelelection. When a question of taxation came up, the Irish party were closured, gagged and evicted from that I Rouse which was supposed to be the greatest Parliament in the world, which was founded by Magna Charter on the law that every man should have justice done to him. The Irish nation 50 years ago numbered nine millions, to-day it numbered q millions. At present Ireland was living under a perpetual coercion act, and the people were being tarred almost 3 millions per annum more than they should be. He took it that most of them present were Irishmen. What brought them there? (a voice" poverty ") The misrule of English Govern- ment in Ireland. There was not an Irishman or Irish- woman that he came across but would rather live at home than anywhere else, but it was the accursed un- just land laws which divorced land and labour' and put the power of evimson into the hands of the landlords and sent their people adrift. They were all exiles there, because of the misgovernment of Ireland, and it was quite natural that they should rally round the cause of Ireland, because they were the men who were fighting the battle in the natural way open to them. He had no quarrel with men who adopted other methods, but it appeared the Constitutional one was the only method which had a chance of success, but if they went OR as they had done, debating Private of speech w ebsipllsee, discussing eft to sinigsup- tphlieems,,t exercising should makecissinhgcniwhateve r righ progress so slow in the House of Commons that the eventuality may occur that the Government would be glad to get rid of them to make their own laws. (Cheers.) He asked them to support the Irish party in the House of Commons, because, out- aide:a few Radical members and Labour members, democracy had 00 representation in the House of Commons. Everybody was represented in the House of ' Commons except the peep e. The fact was Great Britain I was behind every other country in the world in all kinds of legislation, social and economic, which affected the masses of the people, Why ? Because rich men ruled ; ' because the people did not understand their own interests, because the majority of the British working men for some reason or another supported Toryism. Not ' that he was an advocate for what was called Liberalism in the Id 9080 of Commons, because so far as he could ' judge It was six of one and half a dozen of the other. (Cheers.) When the Tories were in the Liberals promised all sorts of things, and when the Libdrals were in the Tories promised something similar, but between the two parties where did the people come in ? (Laughter.) In constqlence of the union of all branches and sections of Irish politicians, they were now a force in the House of Commons, which could not be lightly dispensed with. The Irish Pa rel tirahemo rejounnstgathri,%f repestahhre,tvyl ht h be rißritishga i e of Rouse'cc h o of CD°amoimttmw°raoBtew, eorous and true, ready for battle, and in this constitutionsl s'suggi.. if it had to be followed out, the time may come when they would ride through the ranks as the men at Fontenoy did. (Loud cheers.) There was no fear amonest them, be- cause they knew their cause was just. " Torice armed is he whose cause is just." They had a unite.] people, they had a determined Parliamentary party,and the time had come,when the Irish party,as in the days Of Parnell, would make itself felt in the House of Commons, when they would wring from them the right which belonged to them. (Applause.) They were a nation by race, by religion, by the hand of God, and for his part he would never rest satisfied until they had placed the golden cross and diadem of nation upon their native land and made her a nation once more. (Loud cheers.) Alderman Joyce M P., said he would not have missed what he had seen there that night for a good deal. He had seen one of the most enthusiastic meetings it was ever his lot to see, (Hear, hear.) He always thought the British House of Commons was a famous place; he , could nearly say now, it was an infamous place, I (Laughter). The world heard last week of tho awful scene that was perpetrated in the House of Commons. I 5) there was an awful scene, but it was not caused by 'the Irish Nationalist members. It was caused by the man who led that House, Arthur James Balfour. (Hoot- ing.) Mr Balfour had some arrangement made with the ' backboneless party called the Liberal party, or at least that portion of them represented by the front opposition bench. At 12 o'clock, withnnt a word coming from the Irish benehes, the first Lord of the Treasury moved a vote for 17 millions of money, without a word to be aaid from the Tory and Liberal benches. He made a mistake when be thought it would pass without a word of protest from the Irish benches. They protested and with some effect, and that 17 millions of money was not all for Irish purposes, there was only a little over 2 millions for Irish purposes and the representatives of the masses of the people in England, Scotland and Wales sat like dumb dogs and let the Irish members fiett the battles of the people. They tried to cajole them and failed, they tried to friehten them and failed, they order them out of the House, and the Irish members invited them to come and put them out, and that failed, they would not try it, and he thnught if they had they would have been sick of their job. The finish of it was that 8 or 10 of the Irish members were removed by force. They ordered in their police and they had quite a job, although it was only a passive resistance. There ai ere 50 oil' 60 members left and they told Mr Speaker that they were determined to sit there until

div.head: PIONEER LECTURES AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: PIONEER LECTURES AT EARLESTOWN.

The fourth lecture of the series given by the NAN' ton-in-Makerfleld Lectures Committee, took place on Wednesday evening in the Town Hall, Earles- town. The subject was "The Evolution of Life, or the Contribution of National Science to the Pro- gress of the Century," and the lecturer was Mr F W lieeble, M.A. Mr Thomas Vicars presided and briefly introduced the Lecturer, remarking that he would show his common sense by not saying any- thing on the question of evo'ution. The lecture was profusely illustrated by lime light views which rendered it more interesting and lucid. GOOD TEMPLAR:V.

Hope of Earlestown Lodge meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, Wargrave-road on Monday evening, Bro Williams, C T,presiding. Three candi- dates were proposed and initiated and one member re-admitted. Bro Madan, V D,of St. Helens,briefiy addressed the lodge and tendered the fraternal greetings of the Pioneer Lodge,St.Helens, Bro New- man being responsible for the prugramme, c il!ed upon Bro Huddleston for a song, who responded with " Janey Doyle" ; reading by Sister Ord, " A pot of shamrock ". a brother from Leigh, recitation, "The charge of the light brigade " ; Br, Roberts gave a selection of Irish readings and witticisms; Irish readings by Bro Williamson. The Lodge was closed in the usual manner by Bro Williams, C.T. Sr. JOHN'S PAROCHIAL TEA. AND CONCERT.

Tbe annual parochial tea ari-cfc-O.U.C-eriin conn.c- tion with St John's Church, Earlestown, was held in the Mission Hall on Saturday evening. About 180 people were present,their wants being attended to by the ladies of the congregation, assisted by the wardens and sidesmen. The concert was of an ex- cellent character, and an interesting programme was submitted. There were four tableaux which

were rendered more interestini 1)--y lime light effects They were Four Jolly Smiths," "Faith, Hope and Charity,"" The Japanese Tea-party," and " At the Front." Amongst those taking part were Messrs Brown, Mawdsley, H Mawd.ley and Spencer: Misses S Bunting, I. Ratcliffe, A Horridge, M Harrison. A Clarke, A Beaumont, Templeman, F Hatch, A Clayton, and Mrs Wright. A dialogue, " The Irish servants," Misses Clayton, Martindale, and Camm, Messrs Tucker and Clarke ; quartette "Sweet and low," Mrs Wilson and Mrs Harrison,

Mr Spencer and Rev J C Matthews ; song, "Bed"uin Love Song" Rev J C Matthews; banjo solo " Park Crescent," Miss J Clare (Warrington) ; glee "Jack Frost," choir; piano solo, Mr A Woolcock ; songs " Call Tae back " and "The Soldier's Motto," Rev J C Matthews: EAR,LESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

An entertainment was given at the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown on Saturday evening, to the children of members of the Society, in connection with a distribu'ion of prizes. During the winter months classes have been held at the Co-operative Hall for children with a view of instilling into them the principles of Co-operation and at the close a set of questions was Riven as a kind of examination, prizes being offered on the result. The classes were divided into two section, viz.: for children over ten and under 13 and over 13 and under 16. Eighteen sat for examination in _ section one, and three in

section two. Seven prizes were given in section one and were awarded as follows :—lst, John Thompson, ss: 2nd. Norah Carney, 4s; 3rd, Ellen Littler. 3s; 4th. George Singleton, 2s 6d ; sth, N Blackburne, 2s; 6th, R Fail,ls 6d; 7th, Annie Davies, Is. Section two, two prizes given, Ist. Nellie Huddlesten, 5s ; 2nd, A Jones, 3s. Mr D Forrester presided, and after explaining the objects of the classes proceeded with the distribution of the prizes, as above. A magic lantern entertainment was afterwards given, a number of views being thrown on the screen illustrative of the work of.the Wholesale Co-operative Society in various parts of the country. Several comic slides were also shown, much to the delight of the youngsters. Several songs were given at intervals by Messrs J Gibbons, and J Eluddleston, Miss J Thomas and Eva Jones. Miss Reid accompanied on the piano. After the entertainment each child was presented with a bag of sweets.

Prudential Assurance Company, Limited. Continued progress is reported by this company in the fifty-second annual report which has just been issued, In the ordinary bvanch, the new pol- icies issued during the year numbered 74,680, as- suring the sum of £7,613,035. and producing a new annual premium income of £378,503. The premiums received during the year amounted to .C 3,322,342 being an increase of £177,878 over the preceding year. Life and endowment assurance claims ab- sorbed .E 1,593,150 the beneficiaries numbering about 13,000. At the end of the year there were in force 612,057 policies. In the industrial branch the premiums received during the year were .C 5,447,697 being an iucrease of £278,739, Ind the amount paid in claims was .E 2,227,218 the number of deaths being 221,025,and the matured endowment assurances 2,266. For some years past the Pruden- tial have treated their policy-holders who wish to retirb most liberally. Rather than have lapses free policies are granted to policy-hollers of five years standing and the number thn granted last year was 66,943,bringing no the total in force to 713,634 During the year 17,21.5.0 f these free policies became] claims. There were in force at the close of the year no fewer than 13,891,667 policies in the indw- trial branch, their'average duration being nine and a quarter years—proving the stable character of the business, and reflecting credit on the industrial workers of the country in making provision for the inevitable rainy day. The assets of the company in both branches are .C 39,895,328 being an in- crease of .C 3,063,269 over those of 1899. The investments made by the company are of the highest class. At tne annual meeting of the com- pany, Sir H Harben remarked that there is little difficulty in finding investments, the trouble of selection being the most important factor with which the directors had to contend.
