div.head: EARLESTOWN CRICKET CLUB.
div.p: EARLESTOWN CRICKET CLUB.
The annual general meeting of this club was held in the Viaduct Institute, Earlestown, en Thursday even- ing. ,Mr T Ormani presided, but there was only a moderate attendance of members.

The Secretary (Mr J H Alderson) submitted his report and statement of aceounts, as followe :—"l'he season of 1900 opened with fair prospects, and was on the whole a fairly successful one. Of the 20 lst eleven matches arranged, two were abandoned owing to rain. viz., Leigh (away) and Manchester Clifford (home.) 15 were played, 7 won, as against five in each of the two pre- ceding years, four lost as against 10 and 9in the two previous years, and 7 drawn, we often having the best of the game in those matches, and I feel sure that if the fielding generally had been a little better, we should have had a few more victories to record. The total runs scored by our batsmen were 2.098 for the loss of 138 wickets, an average of 1528 ner wicket ; our orison- ants were credited with 2,236 runs for 161 wickets, averaging 13143. These figures show a large improvement on last year when our wickets only averaged 9104, J Miller heads the batting averages, his figures being 31.6 and though not doing so well early in the season, he latterly batted splendidly. G Husband also batted excellently, being second with an average of 234, and there was ae round improvement, nine batsmen having double figure averages, as compared with four last season. Another sign that the batting im.l proved; is, that the amount paid in talent money wag £4 ss. as against 10s. the year before. I regret that 3 cannot say the same abut the bowling, the wicket t mained averaging 13'143, as against 12'156 lasB season, J H Aldereon's figures reading 63 wickets, average 10 52 W Relanee's 21 wicket" average 132 H Davies, 20 wickets among' 20'7, the latter bowling with rather "hard luck," and t think we can hope for better results in this departmen this season. The second team Played 11 matches, 6 be- ing won, 4 lost, and 1 drawn. This being somewhat the same as last season. R A Robinson and James Hatton came out at the top of the batting averages, both having shown improvement on nast figures, especially the latter. William Harrison is again at the ton of the bowling with an average of 7.19 for 34 wickets. The 4 bats gener- ously presented by the Institute Committee, have been awarded t the following :—G Husband, .7 H Alderson, R A Robinson and W Harrison, and the £2 also kindly given by them, has been divided between T Marsh, W Rylence, James Hatton and J W Burrell, the committee seeming, them next in order of merit. The programme for the coming season will consist of home and home matches with St Helens, Leigh. Manchester Clifford, St , Helena RACI9, Tvldesley, Little Lever, Wigan, Liverpool I and Whalley Range, and the District Junior Match as I]su al . The income for the year amoented to £49 7s 7d ineluding a balance of £1 6; 61, and the expenditure was £49 3s 24 leaving a balance in the Treasurer's hands of 4s sd. Subscriptions realised £29 11' 61 as compared with £29 8; 61, and the gate receipts £l2 12s as against £l7 184 Id, a falling off of £5 6s. A much further aug- mentation of list members is desirable as the subscrip- tion list is one of the most reliable sources of intorno, gate receipts being dependent on the weather and other circumstances, the committee will heartily wel- come any new memlsers. On November 10th a most Allefießolll gathering of members and friends was held at the Viaduct Hotel, on the occasion of a dinner and presentation to cur esteemed late Hon Secretary, Mr John Owen, the presentation taking the form of a hand- some gold watch, as a testimonial to his faithful services for the past 18 years. I believe it ie the hope o! the committee and the members generally that we have inaugurated a regular annual closing dinner. It is with pleasure that I report that the match and practice wickets have been uniformly good throughout the I season, and much credit is due to Mr Josephs, for his management of the ground." The Chairman said their new Secretary was to be I complimented upon the very admirable report he had presented for their consideration. It was very pleasing ' to see that he was endeavouring to tread in the footsteps of his predecessor. Mr Owen, in giving a faithful recog- nition of the services rendered by batters and bowlers, and whatever strictures he had made in his report were for the benefit of other members of the club: He did not make these remarks in any spirit of carping criticism, but in order that the players might be better players in the future, gener;lly, and thus add considerably to the credit of the club. The Secre- tary remarked generally on the fielding of the first team. Had that fielding not been so weak, they would not have had so many drawn matches. He also remarked that subscriptions were not coming in as they might do. There was not that increased membership that there ought to be. considering the advantages and bene- fits which were offered and he thought if every member was deternsined to augment the roll of membership by one, their exchequer would soon increased and they would be able to do better. It must be pleasing to every member of the Committee and the club generally, that they were out of debt for there were no outstanding liabilities so far as he know. That was a fortunate thing for a club of that size and he hoped that the remarks which had been made by the secretary would be appre- ciated, and carried out as far as practicable hv every member of the club and that the future would be in- finitely brighter than the past bad been. There was another feature which was very pleasing and that was that the four presentatimis this year were going to the same winners as last year, viz Messrs. Husband, Alder- son, Roninsem and Harrison, and for the same reasons. Nothing gave the Institute Committee mere pleasure than to give their donation of £2 for prizes, to be awarded as the Committee of the club might deem best.

Mr TF RD erts moved the adoption of the report, which, on being seconded, was carried. Mr Owen said it was remarkable that the bats shauld fall to the same four players. With regard to the bate the committe had no option. It worked automatically. They had a rule that a player must engage in 9 matches and must top averages to secure the prize. The four in question had done that. The committee had for a number of years endeavoured to divide the £2 given by the Institute Cammittee to the best of their ability, and the committee scent a considerable amount of time In irquiring into the doings of the players before awarding the prizes. This year they had heard some criticism upon •h -t they did not think anyone had been wronged. The,- were perfectly certain they did the work to the best of their ability, and they unanimously came to the opinion that the four named were really the best (Applause). The election of office.s was then proceeded with and resulted as follows ;—President, Mr J W Emmett, J P Vice-president. Messrs F Harwood and D Flarrison; treasurer. Mr T Ormand ; secretary, Mr J H Alderson; captain, let team ; Mr 0 W Emmett; vice-captain Ist team, Mr G Husband ; captain 2nd team. AilLimond ; vice-cantain, 2nd team, J Wainwright ; committee. Messrs J Owen, James Seddon, T F Roberts. G Husband J Sanders, II A Robinson, W Jenkinson, F J Reid, and J W Burrell. The prizes offered by the Institute Committee were awarded as follows :-Ist team hatting.G Efusband,bar; let team bowling, J H Alderson, bat; second team b- ring. R A Robinson, bat ; second team bowling, W Harrison, bat. Club awards. left team batting.T Marsh, pair of trousers ; Ist team bowling, W Rvlance, bag ; second team batting, James Hatton, boots; second team bowline. W Burrell, bag. The Chairman moved the thanks of the members to the Secretary and Committee, and Mr John Seddon, in seconding, sugges.ed it would be a good thing if a prize could be offered for the best all round fielding. The Chairman agreed and offered a prize of lOs 6d. Mr A Lirnond taking this offer to be for the first team,rnade a similar offer for the second team.-4 vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the proceedings. DRUNKENNESS AND ITS CURE.

The drink problem has indeed puzzled the statesman, philanthropist, and tiumaqitarian workers Of every class and age. ,‘Sorai suasion h.as tried hard to assuage the evil, and thousands of organizitions and institutions have been started with the same object in view, and yet it is difficult to see that any abiding good has resulted from this avalanche of oratory and organized endeavour A huge army of drunkards and vagrants are marched to the various prisons of the land every year. The sen- tences passed upon these victims of a terrible and uncon- trollable craving for alcoholic stimulants, simply patch them up for another drinking bout, but the miserable and costly game brings no improvement. Indeed, its the case of the habitual drankard—the man or woman in whom the desire for stimulants overrides every other coosideration,—no one really believes that the sentences on imprisonment will have any reforming Influence. And it may be added that very few persons of intelligent mind and humane feeling regard these sufferers from a disease as deserving of punishment. This bettor view arises from the fact that medical scientists of the highest standing have for years urged that drunkenness is a hideous form of disease, rather than a crime. Dr Benjamin Rush nearly a century ago promulgated air; theory and urged that hoqpitals for its exclusive treatment should be established in every city f the land. Dr Norman Kerr, es the result of years of aborious and patient study of inebriety, declares in his plendid work on the subject that intemperance is more of a disease than a crime. The most careful modern research and observation gll tend in the same direction. In the light of the best medical teaching upon alcoholism we see that what we have been in the habit of calling a vile passion is the hungering and thirsting ,S an aboor- mal necessity. Religious sentiment has been much afraid of the term disease as applied to drunkenness, feeling that by so doing we excuse indulgence and con- done debauchery. We have no wish to avoid the moral side of the question, nor to say that sin has not led up ta the disease.

--What we are now chiefly concerned about is r—Has a cure been found for alcoholism. The world is with good reason somewhat sceptical and impatient of the many perfect curia advertized for the drink habit. Within the last few years innumerable specifics have been offered to the world with more or less flourish of trumpets. Are there any of these that have stood the testing fires of lengthering seasons? We very much doubt whether a cure is to be looked for from the mere taking of I a specific. A disease so complicated as alcoholism be- comes must require institutional treatment somewhat akin to that needed for other nerve and mental troubles. Alcoholism and narcotism are now universally admitted Co be a neurosis—a functional disetse—and should have positive medication on the same principles as other and allied nervous and mental troubles. Though it is pro- bably true that no other disease re quires a greater variety of remedial measures, moral, medicinal, and hygenic, combined with sympathy, tact, and skill in meeting the needs of each patient, whether he be most sinner or most sick. This rational, scientific, and efficient method of dealiag with drunkenness must

therefore mean much more than shutting the habitual drunkard up for one, or even two, years in a retreat, in the hope that his craving will die of starvation from liquor. We are not sure that such a course of long separation from old associations ks necessary in 90 per cent of the c tses that would be thus isolated, if proper methods of treatment were adopted for a brief p-riod en the lines of ie Bichloride of gold treatment that has been such a grand success in America for many years. We understand that every state in the union there has now its home where theso medicines and methods are , used, and the United States Government pays to the Keeley Company a royalty for their use in some state homes. The treatment has been attended with similar success in Australia during the last eight years. Though the last 50 years testify to the miasma utter uselessness of mere isolation, or even moral means in the effectual reformation of the confirmed dipsomaniac, this plan which is being strongly urged in many quarters is much more rational and humane than thrusting the poor victims of an inherited or eelf induced disease into gaol. It is simply a monstrous cruelty to arrest a man who is not criminal in ether respects, but whose nervous system is shattered • and his liver kidneys, and other organs .have undergone in- cipient dezederation through continued indulgence in alcoholic liquors and shut him up in gaol, and then forsooth, supp ose he can thus be redeemed from the bondage of an acquired or inherited appe- tite for drink. The moral means and forced detention, however varied and prolonged, have proved insufficient to secure such redemption. What then ? Has medical science while claiming that alcoholism is a disease, failed to discover a remedy ? In view of the' evidence available this seems a belated que3tlon. All over America and Australia and even in this country are ex- patients who have te,tified and are ready to testify that their deliverance has come as a revelation and a bene- diction. Canon Flenning of London, chairman of the Keeley investigation committee, has borne testimony for eight successive years as to the value of the work in England, E Tennyson Smith, Rev Leonard Bite, Mrs Harrison Lee, and many others now in England bear decided testimony to what they know of the good work in Australasia. And yet even stronger testimony Comes from such distinguished citizens of the Colonies as Dr Vance, the D3an of Melbourne, H A Langley, the Archdeacon, Canon Tdcker, Father Robin- son, Rev A R Eiger, Superintendent of the Methodist Central Mission, besides several leading doctors and members of Parliament; and such newspapers as "The Age," " The Herald," &c. This testimony is more em- phatic because those who boar it have been all the Mane, as they state, in close touch with the work there. The principal and pioneer of the work in Australasia told the ministers of the state and the Royal Commission appointed by the Victorian Government to inquire into the subject of dealing with inebriety, when giving his evidence as an expert, that he regarded it as one of the highest duties of the State to provide for s systematic course of treatment for all per- sons addicted to the alcoholic) or morphine habit, "Dipsomania," he says, "is a sort of insanity that needs careful provision and skilful medication and for the sake of the victims and the community at large, Govern- ments most realise a responsibility to help in the great work. -
f

The drunkard Is arrested if he is poor, and when in a sobered,humiliated and nervous state, he is taken before, a justice. The poor dipsomaniac is fined or sent to gaol This cruel treatment aggravates the suffering instead of curing the sufferer. Familiarity with the laws and methods of dealing with inebriates has blinded Us to the monstrous cruelty of locking a man up who is broken lit health,tortured in mind and hopeless in heart, locking him upto consort with criminals instead of providing a suitable place for treating his disease- These are words that ought to have a significance and suggestiveness to the humane promoters and leaders in the establishment of county inebriate homes. Would not these leaders do well to confer with such an expert as Doctor Wolfenden during his sojourn in Southport, and if possible get the benefit of his wide experience and perhaps also a share in his methods and the medicines used in successfully treating alcoholism? The method of cure seems to be a kind of inoculation. The basis of treatment is said to be a molecule of gold, double chloride and sodium, prepared and administered with °that' combinations and auxiliary treatment of hydropathee and hygiene. In from three to five days an aversion for liquor is created and then fairly commences the work of building up the patient's nervous organiza- tion and strengthening his will power, or, as Dr Keeley expressed it when addressing one of his bichloride of gold dubs, "the treatment is continued after the aver- sion Emu; in more entirely to break up the rhythmical habit of a return of the craving for alcohol." No doubt new ground will have to be broken and per- haps some experimental steps takin in order to make the proposed homes for inebriates as efficient as they should be The promoters should spare no pains to get at the hest methods of curative treatment and reforma- tive influence. The homes should of course be amid healthy and cheerful surroundings, with ample Pro- vision for the employment, instruction, and amusement of the patients. Their physical and moral tone must .as far as possible be raised and in order to do this, the bodies must he kept clean and active, their minds as pleasantly occupied as the guiding ingentrty. of the management can arrange by placing within their reach the best facilities for wholesome thought ? In short, all the special curative and helpful remedies that medical science has discovered and brought to bear with success in places like the newly opened Bi-chloride:!pf gold Hydro at Southport should find a congenial sphere in the county and other homes now being projected for Drunkenness.

Warrington Field Club. At the tenth meeting of the winter sessior, held in the Museum Lecture Room, Mr C White pr sided over a crowded assembly to whom Mr C Ger +lett of Manchester, lectured on "Tree Fruits." The subject was illustrated by a long series of most beautiful lantern slades and by a large number of actual fruits and seeds from the lecturer's extensive col- lection. Mr Garnett during the leisure hours of a long and busy life has devoted himself to the accu- mulation and preservation of specimens of fruits and seeds of all kinds of plants from all parts of the world, and was able to show his audience something of the wealth of variety in the modes of reproduc• tion in the vegetable kingdom, as well as the curi- ob't;As of adaptation which fruits and seeds present. The theoretical part of Mr Garnett's discourse did not commend itself to the more critical of his hearers,his notions of design in nature,for instance, being hopelessly confused, but all concurred in ad- miration of the skill and patience exhibited in the examination and preparation of his specimens, and a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the lecturer.

Saturday was almost a blank day on Saturday for Rugby Football in the Warrington district,for the seniors indulged in a rest preparatory to entertaining Leeds Parish Church in the third round of the Cup Competi tion. In order to find the spectators something to do the " A " team " occupied the boards "and lowered the colours of Fletcher's Eogineers by an eleven points margin. Some excellea football was shown on both sides, and the match must be counted as ono of the most interesting displays by junior teams given on the War- rington ground this season. The winners deserved their victory, but it must be remembered on behalf of the 'Engineers that several of their best men have been drafted into the Warrington ranks this season.

There is a fair amount of excitement in the town in. regard to the visit of the Leeds parish' Tiers, and the prevailing opinion appears to be that Warrington will have a harder nut to crack than hitherto. I am inclined to conform to that opinion myself, as I saw the Parish. beat Runcorn at Ir well lane last season—a result which surprised everybody including the winners. They are not as good • lot as the Linnets bat they played with- any amount of dash and a fair quantity of skill. Still,' don't think Warrington have anything to fear. The team that wias at Wilderspool during the remainder of this season will have to be smarter than ordinary.

Just out of curiosity, you know, a couple of Warring- ton committeemen went to Leeds on Saturday in order to see the Parish entertain Bradford. It is quite en the cards that we shall have both the teams to meet and the match between them, was therefore, interesting from a Warrington point of view. Bradford won and thus be: come Yorkshire Ssnior Competition Charnpions,but there was little between the teams. In fact the opinion of the Warrington officials is, I believe, that the losers were the better side. However, such an opinion as that does not count for much. Figures have (40[119 bearing on the matter and I will jast comp re the n clrdi of to day's contestants at Wilderspool. 'nosy are as follows

--- There is not much to chose becween the terns here. The records are practically equal, and the choice of ground is therefore an important factor. It will be noticed that thell'arish have a better defensive record than Warrington.who possess a slight pull on the attack. As that attack has been much improved since the last league match it ought to be good enough for entry into round four.

It is by no means certain that Bradford will be the visitors to Warrington afterwards. They hlve a stiff game to-day with Wakefield Trinity at Wakefield and the Trinitarians possess much the better record in cup- tic contests. Should the Yorkshire champions go down at the cathedral city Warringtoa ought to have a good opportunity of avenging themselves on the Trinity for a knock-out last season but one.

Warrington have chosen the usual team tri oppose Leeds Parish Church. It is as follows : Hallam, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dicke.ison, and Harris, three- quarters; R Bate and Duckworth, ball backs ; Board- man, Edmondson, Swift, Fell, Scholtzs, Eden, Mere- weather, and Cunningham, for wards.
- By the way some people think there are more improb- able things than that VVarringron and Runcorn will appear in the final tie. What ho

Fish ought to beat his previoui record in the scoring line during to-day's encounter. Last season he finished up with 99 points to his c,edit. This season, so far, he has compiled 21 goals, 18 tries, or 96 points and he should easily top the century.

Runcorn are at home to York, the champions of the eastern division of the Yorkshire Second Competition and the conquerors of Elalifax. I look to the Linnets to win by a good margin. They did the right thing in refus- ing to play at York though the bait was the hand- some one of £l2O. They had a duty to their supporters and then the result might have been doubtfnl at York whereas no one feari for the Itunc-irn lads at Irwell lane.

To make common Vegetables more inviting, always serve them with a good Corn Flour sauce. To make such a sauce simply mix a teaspoonful of good Corn Flour with a teacupful of milk, add a teaspoonful of butter, and cook for three minutes. Try such a sauce with the commonest vegetables turnips, carrots, onions, leeks, parsnips, beetroot, &c., and you will be convinced how much they are improved by it.
